Issue Reading note
The largest revenue line appears in no filing AI semiconductor revenue, gigawatts of compute and content per gigawatt are disclosed only on earnings calls. They are unaudited and undefined. The FY2023 base has two management values, $4.2bn implied in December 2023 and $3.8bn stated in December 2024. Every forward figure in Sections 14 and 17 depends on this series.
Segment margins are not GAAP margins Segment operating income excludes stock-based compensation, acquisition-intangible amortization, restructuring and acquisition costs, which Broadcom reports as unallocated. The two segments summed to $41,997m of operating income in FY2025 against $25,484m of reported consolidated operating income. Segment cost of revenue is disclosed only from FY2023, so segment gross-margin history begins there.
FQ3 FY2026 reports on 2 September 2026 That is three weeks after the market data here was struck, and it is the first test of the guided ~74% consolidated gross margin, the roughly 66% semiconductor segment gross margin that guide implies, the $16bn AI line and the +31% software step. Every FY2026 figure is two reported quarters plus one guided quarter.
Fiscal-to-calendar offset Broadcom's quarters run Nov-Jan, Feb-Apr, May-Jul, Aug-Oct, so FY2025 mostly covers calendar 2025. Peer tables in Sections 3, 4 and 16 state the period end for each company; nine of the named peers have non-December year-ends. FY2024's extra week inflates that year's growth rates.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

Broadcom sells two things that share a CEO, a balance sheet and almost nothing else. Semiconductor Solutions designs silicon and has it built by other people: custom AI accelerators to one customer's specification, the Ethernet switches and optical parts that connect them, and a portfolio of mature connectivity, storage and industrial chips. Infrastructure Software sells the virtualization, mainframe and security software Broadcom bought between 2017 and 2023 to large enterprises on three-year contracts. In FY2025 the two produced $36,858m and $27,029m of revenue at 57.6% and 76.8% segment operating margins. By the quarter ended 3 May 2026 semiconductors had grown to 68% of the company.▪

1.1 Semiconductor Solutions

Two customer populations buy this silicon and they behave nothing alike. The AI population is six accounts: Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, and two customers Broadcom has not named. They buy custom accelerators designed to their own architecture plus the switches, fabric routers, NICs, PCIe switches, 1.6T DSPs and lasers that connect them. Purchasing runs through each buyer's silicon organisation across a multi-year roadmap; the alternative at the point of purchase is an NVIDIA GPU or an in-house design. The non-AI population is everything Broadcom sold before 2023: RF front-end and FBAR filters plus Wi-Fi and Bluetooth combination parts into one North American handset maker, set-top-box and PON and DOCSIS silicon into broadband service providers, SAS/RAID and Fibre Channel and disk-drive controllers into server and storage OEMs, enterprise switching, and optocouplers and sensors into industrial customers.

The split between the two comes only from earnings calls.

The series does not extend backwards: FY2023 was described as 15% of segment revenue on the FQ4 FY2023 call, about $4.2bn, and restated to $3.8bn on the FQ4 FY2024 call. Over the three years to FY2026 the AI line added more revenue than the whole segment grew, because the non-AI half shrank $6.8bn on the way. From FY2023 to FY2025 AI added $16,390m while non-AI subtracted $7,714m, so AI supplied 189% of segment growth.▪

1.2 The demand-driver tree

Semiconductor revenue equals accelerator units multiplied by accelerator price, plus networking content attached to those units, plus non-AI end-market demand.▪ Four drivers move those terms. Each is taken past the phrase management uses to the exposure that can be measured independently.

Driver 1 — accelerator volume. Management denominates this in gigawatts of deployed compute, roughly 10 GW planned for shipment in 2027. One level down, that resolves to six named commitments: Google's multi-generation TPU and AI-networking agreement of April 2026 (dollar value undisclosed); Anthropic at over 1 GW in 2026 and a further 5 GW from 2027; OpenAI at 1.3 GW contractually committed for 2027 inside a 10 GW-by-2029 agreement; Meta at 3 GW of MTIA through end-2028 with an initial 1 GW order for delivery in the second half of 2027; and two unnamed customers with $6bn of purchase orders shipping from late 2026 (FQ2 FY2026 call). One level further down, the gigawatts resolve to two things outside Broadcom's control. The first is electrical power and grid interconnection at the customer's site, which Hock Tan says paces deployment: customers are "not just asking for wafers to get the chips on memory... they're also talking about, 'Hey, I got to have the power, the power shell.'" The second is the funding capacity of two counterparties that do not generate the cash to pay for what they have ordered, which is why Broadcom helped assemble a financing vehicle with Apollo, Blackstone and other investors, first tranche $35bn, covering more than 20 GW through 2028. Item 1A of the FY2025 10-K names the same exposure: "Some of these AI customers may have constrained resources or capital and may be unable to pay for their required AI infrastructure and/or seek alternative financings or novel or deferred payment models from their vendors and suppliers." Contribution: accelerators are roughly 60-67% of AI revenue and AI is 72% of segment revenue, so this driver accounts for about 43-48% of the segment against roughly 9% in FY2023.

Driver 2 — content per accelerator. Management calls this "content per gigawatt" and describes it as relatively stable within a generation. One level down, it resolves to three supplier-priced inputs: high-bandwidth memory stacks per package times the HBM contract price, die area at N3 or N2 times the TSMC wafer price, and advanced-packaging cost for a multi-die assembly. Tan's own description of what raises content is a list of purchased inputs — more SRAM, embedded CPU cores, multi-die packages with more HBM — and the CFO describes the memory as a pass-through: "similar to the XPUs where we have memory on those XPUs and we're passing through those costs" (FQ4 FY2025 call). HBM3E contract prices were roughly $13-17 per gigabyte in early 2026, down from a $17-20 peak in the first half of 2025 (siliconanalysts.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]; TSMC N3 wafers are around $20,000 and N2 around $30,000 (siliconanalysts.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. On a 192GB accelerator, memory alone is $2,500-3,300 a unit at contract price [estimate: 192GB at $13-17/GB] against a FY2026 selling price around $12,000-15,000, so between a fifth and a quarter of the price is memory bought from three suppliers. Growth sourced this way earns less than growth from Broadcom's own SerDes and switch silicon.

Driver 3 — networking attach. The measurable exposure is the number of compute nodes to be interconnected times bandwidth per node, and separately whether scale-up stays on copper or moves to optics. Copper favours Broadcom's 200G and 400G SerDes and its PCIe switches; optics favours its 1.6T DSPs, lasers and co-packaged optics. Both are Broadcom, at different margins. Part of this attaches to NVIDIA footprints: Tomahawk 6 is "capturing demand from hyperscalers, whether they use XPUs or GPUs" (FQ2 FY2026 call). Networking therefore sells against total accelerator deployment, a wider base than Broadcom's custom-silicon share. Contribution: about 40% of FQ2 FY2026 AI revenue, roughly $4.3bn in the quarter, growing 60% year on year in FQ1 FY2026.

Driver 4 — non-AI end markets. Management calls this "the cycle". One level down it resolves by sub-market: wireless, roughly 45% of the non-AI half, is one North American handset maker's build volume times RF, FBAR, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth and touch content per handset; broadband, roughly 14%, is service-provider access capital spending on PON, DOCSIS and set-top; server storage, roughly 20%, is enterprise on-premises server shipments and SAS/RAID and Fibre Channel attach; enterprise networking and industrial, roughly 20% together, are campus switching refresh and factory automation. Those weights come from [estimate: FY2024 end-market dollars disclosed on the FQ4 FY2024 call, the last period Broadcom gave them] and are three fiscal years old.

Against the realized record. Two of the four drivers behave differently from the way management describes them.

Accelerator volume is a weaker near-term driver than the gigawatt framing implies. Accelerator revenue grows about 2.7x from FY2025 to FY2026 while units grow about 1.1-1.3x, so most of the increase is price per unit▪ [estimate: disclosed AI revenue times the 60-67% accelerator share, divided by third-party unit and ASP estimates of roughly 2.0-2.6m units at $5,000-6,500 in FY2025 and 2.3-2.9m at $12,000-15,000 in FY2026; the unit count comes from third-party estimates and the ASP share of the increase ranges from about 75% to 92% across the bounds]. Tan says the same thing in mechanism terms: "you're driving less chips, though the ASP of each chip is going up in price" (FQ2 FY2026 call).

Non-AI is a claimed driver that has not appeared for two years. In December 2024 management declared a bottom and a recovery: "we saw a cyclical bottom in fiscal '24 at $17.8 billion. We expect a recovery from this level and the industry's historical growth rate of mid-single digits" (FQ4 FY2024 call). FY2025 non-AI came in at $16,668m, below the declared floor. FY2026 is tracking about $17.6bn, still below FY2024 in the third year after that call. Non-AI supplied minus 89% of FY2023-FY2025 segment growth. The first supporting evidence for the recovery arrived in FQ2 FY2026, when non-AI bookings exceeded $6bn against $4.2bn shipped and FQ3 was guided to $4.5bn, up 12% year on year.

Non-AI end-market detail has not been published since December 2024, so which of wireless, broadband, server storage and industrial is recovering and which is being designed out is unknown. The most recent end-market figures are FY2024.

The reconciliation to the reported figure closes. AI revenue of $10,800m at an estimated 70.7% gross margin plus non-AI revenue of $4,209m at an estimated 66.4% gives $4,579m of cost of revenue against $4,573m as filed, a 0.1% overshoot. The accelerator bill of materials — memory at $2,500-3,300, logic die at $700-1,200, substrate and advanced packaging and test at $900-2,000 — sums to $4,100-6,500 and implies a 46-73% gross margin at the price range, centred 57-66%, against 64-68% from the residual solve. The two overlap at 64-66%.

The non-AI row is blank because the inputs do not exist. Broadcom stopped disclosing end-market revenue when it moved to AI-versus-non-AI reporting in December 2024, it has never disclosed units, prices or attach rates for wireless, broadband, server storage or industrial, and no supplier or customer filing constrains them, because the handset customer, the broadband service providers and the storage OEMs are diversified buyers who do not break out Broadcom content.

Cost of revenue is wafers from TSMC (about 95% of contract-manufactured wafers in FY2025), assembly and test at ASE, Foxconn, Amkor and SPIL, memory bought for accelerator packages, substrates and advanced packaging, and the fixed cost of Broadcom's own FBAR and III-V fabs in Fort Collins, Breinigsville and Singapore. More than three-quarters of FY2026 manufacturing materials come from five suppliers, some of them single-source (10-Q FQ1 FY2026 Item 1A).

Operating expense is close to fixed and cost of revenue is close to fully variable. FQ2 FY2026 R&D and SG&A of $1,155m grew 19% year on year against segment revenue growth of 79%, and operating expense declined from 11.5% of revenue to 7.7% in four quarters. Broadcom owns almost no leading-edge capacity, so wafer, memory and packaging cost scales one-for-one with units. That combination produced a seven-year realized incremental operating margin of 67% (FY2018 to FY2025, $11,979m of additional segment operating income on $17,790m of additional revenue), and the AI-era quarters are landing at 66-68%, the same rate the segment delivered through the 2021-22 non-AI upcycle.▪ The AI mix has raised the volume passing through those economics without improving them.

The margins above exclude stock-based compensation, which is unallocated. Consolidated R&D of $5,960m for the first half of FY2026 against segment R&D of $3,118m implies $2,842m of stock compensation inside R&D alone; allocating the semiconductor share of that plus SG&A takes the half-year segment operating margin from the filed 61.0% to roughly 53.7%▪ [estimate: allocation on segment R&D and SG&A shares; a minimum, because cost-of-revenue stock compensation is not separable].

1.5 Infrastructure Software

Four software portfolios plus one hardware line, all inside one reportable segment: Private Cloud (VMware Cloud Foundation, latest release 9.1, with vSphere Foundation, Telco Cloud, Private AI, Live Recovery, vDefend, Avi Load Balancer and Tanzu), Mainframe Software (CA), Cybersecurity (Symantec and Carbon Black), Enterprise Software (AIOps, DevOps, value stream management) and Fibre Channel SAN switches, modules and management software, which is physical hardware booked inside the software segment. The FY2024 10-K named eight portfolios; Tanzu and Application Networking & Security were folded into Private Cloud for FY2025, and VeloCloud was sold to Arista in June 2025 for $300.0m in cash (ANET 10-K FY2025). Broadcom attaches revenue to none of the five.

Buyers are large enterprises and government agencies, "including most of the Fortune 500" (10-K FY2025 Item 1). VMware has approximately 300,000 customers on management's figure; Broadcom manages the largest 10,000 directly and pushes the rest to partners (FQ3 FY2025 call). The alternative at the point of purchase is re-platforming a production virtual-machine estate onto Nutanix AHV, Microsoft Hyper-V, Red Hat OpenShift, Proxmox or a public cloud.

One term swings segment revenue, and it is set at signature. Arrangements without termination-for-convenience rights let Broadcom recognize the licence portion upfront on transfer of control; arrangements with those rights are recognized ratably.▪

FY2024 4,601 21,478 21.4% 16,877
FY2025 7,800 27,029 28.9% 19,229
FQ1 FY2026 1,755 6,796 25.8% 5,041
FQ2 FY2026 1,964 7,178 27.4% 5,214

Sources: 10-K FY2025 Note 3; 10-Q FQ2 FY2026 Note 2. The quarterly figures are derived by subtracting the disclosed FQ2 amount from the disclosed half-year total.

Splitting the segment requires estimation. The FY2024 10-K disclosed that VMware contributed $12,384m of net revenue that year, leaving $9,094m for the legacy portfolios. Applying a 10-20% legacy decline to that base gives FY2025 legacy plus Fibre Channel SAN of $7,275-8,185m and VMware of $18,844-19,754m [estimate]. Fibre Channel SAN can be sized on its own: the FY2018 segment was Brocade's SAN business alone at $1,780m of revenue and a 65.0% operating margin, which puts it at roughly $1.4-2.2bn now, about 6-8% of the segment [estimate].

Five terms drive software revenue and two of them move it.

  • Licensed core base. VCF is licensed per physical CPU core with a minimum of 16 core licences per processor (Broadcom KB 313548, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. The measurable exposure is enterprise x86 sockets running ESXi times cores per socket times paid-subscription retention. The middle term is set by AMD and Intel roadmaps: top-bin EPYC went from 64 cores in 2019-21 to 128 and 192 in 2024, and Xeon from 28 cores in 2019 to 128 performance cores in 2024, so a customer refreshing a two-socket server without changing socket count multiplies its licence bill by the core-count ratio. Tan named this on the FQ2 FY2026 call as the reason software growth is accelerating. The third term runs the other way: Broadcom retired the perpetual model and the free hypervisor tier, raised order minimums, and moved roughly 290,000 of 300,000 accounts to partners.
  • Realized price per core-year. This driver produced the growth, as a one-time step. Customers on vSphere alone were moved to the full VCF stack, and list prices and minimum quantities rose. VCF adoption among the largest 10,000 customers went from below 10% pre-acquisition to about 70% at FQ1 FY2025, over 87% at FQ2 and "way over 90%" at FQ3 FY2025. Gartner's Paul Delory told the firm's Sydney conference on 12 May 2026 that VMware licensing bills "typically rise by 300 to 400 percent" under the VCF-only model (theregister.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Tan gave the timing on the FQ2 FY2025 call: contracts run about three years and the renewal wave was "2/3 of the way", placing completion around late calendar 2026.
  • Contract structure. Upfront licence revenue rose $3,199m in FY2025 against a segment revenue increase of $5,551m, so 58% of the year's incremental revenue came from a larger upfront-recognized component.▪ Whether a customer signs away its termination right is a negotiation outcome at signature, and 64% of contract liabilities at 3 May 2026 related to contracts that retain those rights.
  • Renewal cohort timing sets the quarterly shape. Legacy portfolio decay is the offset: solving the two growth rates management disclosed for FQ1 FY2026 (segment +1%, VMware +13%) puts the non-VMware portfolios down 16-33% year on year depending on VMware's share of the base, with 20-26% the central range [estimate: two disclosed growth rates solved across a VMware base share of 60-75%].

Reported growth splits into the upfront piece and everything else. In FQ1 FY2026 upfront licence revenue declined $217m year on year while non-upfront revenue grew 6.5%, producing +1.4% reported; in FQ2 upfront recovered to +8.9% and non-upfront grew 8.8%, producing +8.8% reported. The underlying business grew 6.5-8.8% in both quarters. Upfront licence revenue, which produced 58% of FY2025's growth, contributed nothing in the first half of FY2026, and reported growth moved with it.

1.6 Software unit economics

Unit Units Realized price per unit-year Input cost per unit Gross profit per unit Implied gross margin Reconciliation
Directly-managed VCF enterprise account ~9,000-10,000 (top 10,000 customers, over 90% on VCF) $1.4-1.7m [estimate] $98-119k [estimate] $1.3-1.6m 93.0% Segment cost of revenue $1,902m on $27,029m equals 7.0%; management stated 93% on both FY2026 calls
Legacy portfolios (mainframe, cybersecurity, enterprise software) not disclosed not disclosed not disclosed not disclosed not disclosed Revenue $5.5-6.5bn [estimate]; no supplier, customer or physical anchor constrains mainframe MIPS or endpoint seats
Fibre Channel SAN switches and modules not disclosed not disclosed ~32-40% of segment cost of revenue — 60-68% [estimate] Revenue $1.4-2.2bn [estimate]; absorbs $608-760m of the segment's $1,902m of cost of revenue

The blended 93.0% decomposes. Fibre Channel SAN at $1.4-2.2bn of revenue and a 60-68% gross margin consumes $608-760m of segment cost of revenue, leaving $1,142-1,294m to support $24.8-25.4bn of software revenue, an implied software-only gross margin of about 95%. The reported 93.0% is therefore roughly 95% software blended with roughly 64% hardware.

The two routes to a price per core do not meet. Working down from revenue at a realized $185-275 per core-year implies 57-85 million licensed cores; working up from an installed base of roughly 1.0-1.3bn enterprise cores at about 70% virtualized and about 65% VMware share implies 400-500 million cores under VMware management. Only a minority of the estate VMware manages is under a current paid subscription at anything near published pricing, and the blended realized price across the whole paying book is on the order of $75-150 per core-year [estimate: VMware revenue of $18.8-19.8bn at roughly 85% subscription share, over a paying base of 90-270m cores], well below the $350-400 list. Both can hold at once: customers who stayed on the full stack saw the multiple-hundred-percent increase Gartner describes, while the blended average is pulled down by legacy support renewals and by very large estates on deep discounts.

Incremental margins here exceed 100%, which is not operating leverage on a fixed base. Total segment cost declined 16.5% in FY2025 while revenue rose 25.8%. R&D declined 9.8% year on year in FQ1 FY2026 and 11.2% in FQ2; SG&A declined 27.2% in FY2025 and a further 8-10% in each of the last two quarters. Broadcom's entire software segment — VMware plus mainframe plus Symantec plus enterprise software plus Fibre Channel SAN — spent $767m less on R&D in FY2025 than VMware alone spent in its final standalone year, on roughly twice the revenue, and the FQ2 FY2026 run-rate annualizes to $2,404m and is still declining.▪ Headcount across the whole company went from about 20,000 before VMware to about 37,000 at close and about 33,000 at 2 November 2025.

Fully loading the segment for stock compensation puts the margin where management said it would be. Allocating FY2025's $7,568m of unallocated stock compensation on revenue share gives 65.0%; allocating on segment operating expense share gives 62.0% [estimate]. Tom Krause on the VMware announcement call, 26 May 2022: "we can grow our top-line revenues at mid-single digits percentage on a recurring basis, if not faster, while driving EBITDA margins in the mid-60s%."

1.8 Capital and working capital

Capital intensity is close to the lowest in the industry, because the leading-edge capital burden is at TSMC. Consolidated capital expenditure was $623m in FY2025, 1.0% of revenue and 1.09x that year's depreciation.▪ It doubled year on year in the first half of FY2026 to $481m as the Singapore advanced-packaging facility builds, and the FY2025 10-K states FY2026 capital expenditure will be higher, but from a 1% base. Broadcom's invested capital is $97,801m of goodwill and $28,333m of net intangibles, all of it from acquisitions.

Working capital is where the AI ramp shows up, and it turned in two quarters.

Inventory nearly doubled in six months with finished goods up 2.7x. Spears frames the build as deliberate: securing supply "in anticipation of accelerating AI semiconductor growth in the second half of the year" (FQ2 FY2026 call). Over the same half Broadcom sold $2,350m of receivables under its factoring arrangements against $3,951m a year earlier, so the record 46% free-cash-flow margin was delivered while receivable pull-forward halved. Customer prepayments of $14,242m still exceed receivables of $10,830m.

One disclosure in FQ2 FY2026 changed the cost model. Unconditional, non-cancelable purchase commitments went from $132m at 2 November 2025 and $54m at 1 February 2026 to $128,110m at 3 May 2026, scheduled $22m in the FY2026 remainder, $55,214m in FY2027, $72,870m in FY2028 and $4m in FY2029.▪ The definition did not change between filings. Committed purchases for the rest of FY2026 are $22m, so none of this is near-term inventory; it is FY2027 and FY2028 capacity bought outright. The same quarter's revenue note attributes the step in remaining performance obligations to "a long-term contract for custom AI accelerators entered in the fiscal quarter ended May 3, 2026", so the customer commitment and the supplier commitment were signed together. The counterparties are almost certainly not TSMC: the same 10-Q's risk factors still state that Broadcom does "not generally have long-term capacity commitments with our CMs" and buys "on a purchase order basis with no minimum quantities", while what Tan described locking up is memory, substrates and glass. Neither the FQ2 FY2026 call nor the 10-Q's management discussion mentions the schedule.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

Broadcom sells across roughly two dozen product lines and the technologies underneath them differentiate to very different degrees, grouped here by the strength of the evidence.

Group Technologies Strongest observable
Hard to replicate Custom accelerator design flow; high-speed SerDes; Tomahawk Ethernet switch silicon; Jericho deep-buffer routers; FBAR filters; disk-drive preamplifiers First to market at 102.4 Tb/s in June 2025 and still the only 100T-class Ethernet switch shipping a year later
Real but narrower PCIe switching; Thor NICs; VCSEL, EML and PAM4 DSP optics; DOCSIS, PON and Wi-Fi SoCs; SAS/RAID and Fibre Channel About 70% Fibre Channel switch share held for a decade; over 80% of Wi-Fi 6 access-point infrastructure
Weak or contested Co-packaged optics; Wi-Fi/Bluetooth combination silicon; the patent estate Apple replaced Broadcom's combination chip with its own N1 across the iPhone 17 line; the disclosed patent estate declined 32% between FY2020 and FY2023
Not technology VMware Cloud Foundation; mainframe software; Symantec 93% gross margin on a hypervisor with credible free substitutes

The head of the ASIC division described what Broadcom sells: the customer supplies the compute architecture and Broadcom supplies everything else plus a proven path to volume. "The customer brings their engine, the architecture... we build a Ferrari, we put the wheels on, we put the chassis... We just connect the engine and hit the gas" (Deutsche Bank custom-silicon webinar, 19 April 2022).

The custom accelerator platform. Broadcom does not design the accelerator. The customer supplies the matrix-multiply arrays, the sparsity handling and the numerics. Broadcom supplies a pre-qualified library of hard IP blocks — SerDes, memory controllers, PCIe, die-to-die interconnect, processor cores — an automated physical-design flow, packaging already proven thermally and mechanically, and volume manufacturing. The flow is the product, and it is re-earned at each process node: Broadcom ports the flow to a new node, debugs it on the first two or three chips, then reuses the debugged flow for the next fifty to ninety.▪ Frank Ostojic put the mechanism plainly at the same webinar: "By the time we're in the fourth chip, we have an improved flow that is fully adapted to 5 nm." A firm doing two or three chips per node never reaches a proven flow before the node changes. Broadcom taped out 120 chips a year company-wide as of 2022, with 20 designs at 5nm and 10 in development at 3nm, and about 60 designs running concurrently [deck: Deutsche Bank custom-silicon teach-in 2022-04-19, slides 13-15]. The second barrier is analog content implemented in ordinary deep-submicron CMOS, which is what allows data converters, regulators and drivers to be integrated onto the same die as the digital logic. The third is packaging: warpage, delamination, thermal integrity and power delivery on 3,000+ mm² of stacked silicon take years to solve.

What the customer keeps and what Broadcom keeps was drawn explicitly at the 2024 investor meeting: the customer owns the processing-unit architecture, and Broadcom owns the design flow and performance optimization, the HBM physical layer and integration, the network IO architecture and chiplets, and the 2.5D, 3D and silicon-photonics packaging [deck: Broadcom Investor Meeting 2024-03-20, slide 87]. Engagement depth was shown on the next slide: one customer at ten years and ten co-developed accelerators, a second at four years and four, both with the following generation already in architecture [deck: same, slide 89]. Design start to tape-out runs seven to nine months, first silicon to production within six months, and architecture freeze to volume ramp within eighteen.

This differentiation buys volume and visibility, and it does not convert to price.▪ Ostojic's division "earns pretty much the corporate average on semiconductor product margins" at the operating line (Tan, April 2022), and the CFO confirmed in FQ2 FY2026 that "our ASICs, TPUs, some of the wireless business has lower margins" at the gross line, offset by the richer networking half.

SerDes. A serializer-deserializer converts parallel on-chip data into a serial stream and back, and it sets how far a signal travels over copper before optics become necessary. Optics are the second-largest source of power and cost in an AI cluster after the accelerators themselves: a one-million-accelerator cluster contains roughly ten million high-speed links (Vijay Janapaty, Investor Meeting 2024). The design objective follows. Peregrine, the 5nm 100G SerDes, drives 45 dB backplane channels and 4-metre direct-attach copper cables against an IEEE standard of 2 metres, and includes native optical equalization so a switch can drive an optical module without a separate retimer. Condor, the 3nm 200G part, holds 45+ dB and 2+ metre copper reach at double the rate. A 400G SerDes was described as running in the lab by FQ1 FY2026 with a 2028 step-up. Making one SerDes work is a demonstration; making 512 of them work simultaneously on one die at yield is the barrier, and Tomahawk 5 integrates 512 lanes of 100G. Broadcom develops its SerDes concurrently with TSMC's process development, which is the operational meaning of the disclosure that approximately 95% of its contract-manufactured wafers come from TSMC.

Tomahawk and Jericho. Tomahawk is a fixed-function, high-radix Ethernet switch chip paired with an intelligent NIC that schedules traffic at the endpoint; Jericho is the opposite arrangement, an intelligent deep-buffer switch paired with an ordinary NIC, for customers with heterogeneous NIC fleets. The performance problem being solved is accelerator idle time: Meta data presented at OCP showed traffic sitting in the network 18% to 57% of the time on large training runs, which on a 100,000-GPU cluster at $20,000-30,000 per GPU is $2bn-3bn of infrastructure idle for that fraction of the time.

Product Capacity Shipped
Tomahawk 4 25.6 Tb/s 2019-2020
Tomahawk 5 51.2 Tb/s late 2023
Tomahawk 6 102.4 Tb/s June 2025
Tomahawk Ultra 51.2 Tb/s, 250 ns latency July 2025
Tomahawk 6 Davisson 102.4 Tb/s with co-packaged optics October 2025
Tomahawk 7 ~200 Tb/s taped out FQ2 FY2026, launch 2027
Jericho3-AI 32,000 accelerators ~late 2022

Sources: Broadcom press releases via GlobeNewswire, accessed 2026-08-14 [web]; FQ3 FY2025 and FQ2 FY2026 calls. Bandwidth has doubled every 18-24 months across five generations, and Broadcom has shipped ahead of its announced dates twice: Tomahawk 5 was guided in March 2023 to launch in early 2024 and shipped in late 2023, and Tomahawk 6 was targeted for late 2025 and shipped in June 2025.▪

Seven of the eight largest AI clusters in deployment used Broadcom Ethernet as of June 2024, and AI switch order backlog was above $10,000m at FY2025 year-end.▪ Independently, Dell'Oro reported that Ethernet switch sales in AI back-end networks more than doubled and accounted for about two-thirds of data-centre switch sales in AI clusters in the first quarter of 2026 (delloro.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web].

Where the technology is contested. PCIe switching is a live challenge to a position Broadcom has held for twenty years across five generations.▪ Astera Labs moved from retimers into switching: its Scorpio P-Series has shipped since the second quarter of 2025 with design wins at three hyperscalers and two more starting late 2026, and a 320-lane Scorpio X-Series announced on 5 May 2026 is shipping to hyperscalers for a second-half 2026 ramp (servethehome.com and asteralabs.com/news, both accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Its differentiation is architectural — in-network compute engines that offload collective operations from the accelerators — and it reached hyperscaler design wins inside five years, which is the counter-example to the claim that continuity and scale are sufficient barriers everywhere.

Scale-up is the contest that matters more. The fabric inside a rack has been NVIDIA's proprietary NVLink, and three open alternatives compete: UALink, NVLink Fusion (NVIDIA opening its own fabric to Marvell, Fujitsu, Qualcomm and Astera Labs), and Ethernet-based scale-up under the OCP ESUN effort. Broadcom left UALink and backs Ethernet alone: "What is really open source and open standards is Ethernet. And we believe Ethernet will prevail as it does" (Tan, FQ2 FY2025 call). Marvell has committed to supporting all three on its scale-up fabric devices, which is a hedge Broadcom has not taken. The leading indicator that Ethernet scale-up is losing would be an accelerator customer specifying UALink or NVLink Fusion for a Broadcom-designed part.

Broadcom's most-advertised optical technology is being deprioritised by its own CEO in favour of a different Broadcom product. On co-packaged optics: "you don't need to go run into some bright shiny objects called CPO, even as we are the lead in CPO. CPOs will come in its time, not this year, maybe not next year" (FQ1 FY2026 call), in the same remarks in which he said 400G SerDes will keep accelerator customers on direct-attach copper through 2028. Broadcom wins either way, and no co-packaged-optics revenue has been disclosed in any filing or on any call.

Where the technology already failed. Apple's in-house N1 networking chip shipped in the iPhone 17 in September 2025, replacing Broadcom's Wi-Fi and Bluetooth combination part after debuting in Apple TV and HomePod mini earlier that year (macrumors.com and techspot.com, both accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Bernstein estimated the revenue effect at $1,000m-1,500m; Broadcom has never quantified it. Apple retained Broadcom's filter content. Broadcom's position held where the process is proprietary and made in its own fab, and gave way where the technology was standard CMOS integration a well-resourced customer could reproduce.▪

What sustains the lead, and the number that questions it. Cash R&D grew 1.8% year on year in FY2025 while AI semiconductor revenue grew 65%.▪ GAAP R&D of $10,977m less $5,020m of stock compensation is $5,957m against $5,850m in FY2024, and R&D excluding stock compensation declined from 11.3% of revenue to 9.3%. The FY2025 10-K says why directly: "Research and development expense increased $1,667 million, or 18%, in fiscal year 2025... The increase was primarily due to higher stock-based compensation." R&D headcount went from roughly 20,400 to roughly 18,800 over the same year. Two explanations fit. Either the reusable flow and IP library let one investment serve 17 semiconductor divisions, which is what management claims and what the tape-out cadence supports, or the engineering base is being underfunded and the lead will narrow. The Tomahawk 7 launch date in 2027 and the 400G SerDes date in 2028 are both on public record and both distinguish the two.

Infrastructure software. The segment has no technical differentiator of this kind and its economics do not depend on one. VMware Cloud Foundation is described by management as "the permanent abstraction layer between AI software and physical chips" that "cannot be disintermediated or replaced" (FQ1 FY2026 call). A type-1 hypervisor has free substitutes (KVM, Proxmox), commercial substitutes (Nutanix AHV, Hyper-V, Red Hat) and hyperscaler substitutes. What differentiates the segment is contract structure and the cost of migrating a production virtual-machine estate.▪ The mainframe portfolio is a cleaner switching-cost asset: Broadcom, IBM and BMC are the only meaningful vendors in a market Broadcom's own general manager sized at about $7bn, where migrations are "measured in years".

The patent estate is not the moat and the 10-K says so: "We are not substantially dependent on any single patent or group of related patents." The disclosed count went 22,774 (FY2020), 19,170, 17,035, 15,400, 20,870 with VMware, and approximately 19,000 at 2 November 2025, with the June 2026 investor deck showing approximately 18,000 six months later [deck: Q2 FY2026 company overview 2026-06-03, slide 3]. What the portfolio protects is the internal IP-core library, which is an engineering-capability asset.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

3.1 Semiconductor Solutions

Broadcom's semiconductor franchise earns returns far above any plausible cost of capital and has done so for eight consecutive years, and its durability is open to erosion by the six customers who now account for roughly half of it.▪ Segment operating margin went from 48.5% in FY2018 to 57.6% in FY2025 and 61.8% in the quarter ended 3 May 2026, on a segment gross margin that has stayed inside a 67-70% band since FY2023 while segment revenue grew 79% year on year. Company-wide capital expenditure in that quarter was $231m, about 1% of revenue, so almost none of the profit is consumed by reinvestment in plant.

The barrier was built over three decades. The design flow is re-ported from node to node and amortized across fifty to ninety chips per platform, against a company running 120 tape-outs a year. A customer starting from nothing needs two or three chips per node simply to find the flow's failure modes, by which time the node has moved on. That is a continuity advantage defended by out-executing, and it excludes nobody by contract or by law.▪

Three facts limit how long it holds. Apple was disclosed as approximately 20% of Broadcom's net revenue in each of FY2021, FY2022 and FY2023, then designed Broadcom's Wi-Fi and Bluetooth combination chip out of the iPhone 17 with its own part in 2025; the FY2024 and FY2025 10-Ks stopped naming Apple. Hock Tan said on 3 June 2026 that Google, the largest custom-accelerator customer on every published estimate, will source elsewhere as well: "we fully expect that there will be some diversity of sources for them. But our commitment from them is a very substantial dollar mark." And the FY2025 10-K rewrote a competition sentence unchanged since FY2018 to add four words: competition will increase "as new companies, including some of our customers, enter the markets."

Concentration moved sharply over the same period. The top five end customers went from approximately 40% of net revenue in FY2025 to approximately 50% in the quarter ended 1 February 2026 and 45% across the first half of FY2026, and the distributor channel from 48% to 56%. Six buyers now account for roughly half the company, each with the balance sheet and the internal silicon staff to fund a second source.▪ Broadcom is also not raising price per unit of delivered compute: Tan on 3 June 2026 said dollars per gigawatt "is relatively stable. But the number of gigawatts will keep -- will accelerate," explaining that chip count per gigawatt falls as the price of each chip rises.

Management claims: the framing sentence of the FY2025 10-K is "We combine global scale, engineering depth, broad product portfolio, superior execution and operational focus." The specific moat claim comes from the ASIC division: "No ASIC provider in the industry has this scale, this continuity, this efficiency, and this predictability" (Ostojic, April 2022), and Tan's version of the entry barrier: "There is continuity and what they call sustainability. You just can't show up one day and do one." On customer-owned tooling: "we are by far way out there. And we will not see competition in COT for many years to come" (FQ1 FY2026 call). Item 1 states that Broadcom is "not substantially dependent on any single patent," and the FY2025 competition section names no competitor at all.

External sources: the sell-side digest holds six Broadcom-touching reports, all between 29 June and 27 July 2026. Morgan Stanley's 14 July note is titled "In Defense of AVGO's ASIC Share" and models Broadcom retaining roughly 80% of TPU volume over time, describing bear cases at 50% as premature, after the share question had already driven year-to-date underperformance. Barclays on 24 July models roughly 10 GW of calendar-2027 deployments at about $15bn per gigawatt and expects content per gigawatt to rise, which contradicts Tan's own "relatively stable" statement. Trade press reports Google splitting the next TPU generation between Broadcom and MediaTek and adding Marvell on networking ASICs (digitimes.com and wccftech.com, both accessed 2026-08-14) [web, unverified — the share figures in those reports come from unnamed supply-chain contacts and disagree with Morgan Stanley's estimate]. Harlan Sur of JPMorgan put his own estimate of customer-owned-tooling programmes to management on 4 March 2026 — roughly half the performance, half the complexity, twelve to eighteen months behind — and management did not dispute it.

Ground-up view: this segment is two economically different businesses. Custom accelerators are a design-services and IP-licensing business dressed as a product business, where buyer power is unusually high: there are six buyers, each has more cash than Broadcom, each employs silicon architects, and each has a strategic reason to avoid a single source for its most expensive input. The customer owns the architecture, so what it buys is implementation, which is what a rival implementation house can bid for, and the switching cost spans one programme generation. Merchant AI networking is a standard-parts business with a real standards-based network effect: Ethernet's value to a buyer rises with how many other buyers use it, because switch, NIC, optics and cable vendors all target the same standard, and Broadcom benefits from every hyperscaler that wants an alternative to a single vendor.▪ Networking is the more portable of the two advantages and the higher-margin one. Non-AI semiconductors behave as a mature portfolio of narrow positions, with FBAR the one place with a process-based barrier instead of a design-based one.

Each claimed source of advantage, with the evidence on both sides:

Claimed advantage Evidence for Evidence against Does it pass
Scale in IP and design methodology Segment operating expense declined from 10.5% of segment revenue to 7.7% while revenue grew 79%; incremental segment operating margin of 67.8% on the FQ2 year-on-year step Segment gross margin of 69.5% is still below FY2023's 70.0%, so the widening is at the operating line only Yes, at the operating line
Switching costs on custom programmes Remaining performance obligations of $164.6bn at 3 May 2026 on firmly committed contracts, from $33.3bn at FY2025 year-end; six multi-generation customer agreements Google multi-sourcing confirmed by the CEO; Apple's connectivity design-out completed Partly, one generation deep
Network effects in Ethernet Networking reached almost 40% of AI revenue against management's expected 30%, and sells into non-Broadcom accelerator and GPU footprints Management expects reversion toward 30%; no disclosed share or attach series exists to test compounding Partly
IP and patents Approximately 19,000 issued patents The 10-K states no substantial dependence on any patent; competitors design around at the architecture level No
Distribution One distributor at 42% of net revenue That concentration is leverage over Broadcom No
Cost position Segment gross margin held 67-70% through leading-edge wafer and memory tightness Content per gigawatt described as stable, so realized price per unit of delivered compute is not rising Cost pass-through holds; price escalation does not
Process technology (FBAR, InP) Sole-source internal fabs at Fort Collins and Breinigsville; Apple retained filter content after replacing the combination chip Confined to wireless and optics, inside the flat non-AI half Yes, and small
Data, brand, regulation Not claimed Export controls constrain Broadcom instead of protecting it No

Return on invested capital. The chief operating decision maker does not evaluate segment assets, so no segment balance sheet exists. Segment goodwill was $26,013m at 2 November 2025 against $71,788m assigned to software; company-wide net property was $2,530m and inventory $2,270m. Adding segment-attributable receivables gives invested capital of roughly $33-37bn; allocating stock compensation on the segment's share of operating expense and taxing at management's guided 16% gives NOPAT of about $14.8bn, so segment return on invested capital is roughly 40-45%▪ [estimate: allocation of receivables, payables and stock compensation is not disclosed and drives the range]. Consolidated GAAP return on invested capital was 16.9% in FY2025 on a 15% normalised tax rate. The gap between the two is VMware goodwill in the other segment.

Four differences between the fiscal-year and quarterly comparisons matter. Broadcom's own segment runs 4.2 points of operating margin above its FY2025 row, so the latest quarter is better than the fiscal year. Marvell's FY2026 row at 16.1% and its latest quarter at 14.0% both differ sharply from FY2025's −12.5%, which absorbed goodwill and restructuring charges; the latest quarter confirms the FY2026 level. Qualcomm, Skyworks and Qorvo are all in year-on-year revenue decline in the latest quarter while their fiscal-year rows show flat-to-positive growth, so the handset RF and connectivity market Broadcom's non-AI half shares with them is contracting now. And Credo at 68.5% and Astera at 73.3% show that a small focused entrant reaches Broadcom's gross margin; the 25-to-39-point operating-margin gap between them and Broadcom comes from R&D intensity of 20-36% against 6.7%, which is what the scale advantage buys.▪

Over time. Against NVIDIA the gap has moved against Broadcom. On a basis that adds stock compensation back to NVIDIA and leaves Broadcom's segment margin as reported, Broadcom's semiconductor segment operating margin was 53.8% in FY2021 against NVIDIA's 35.6% in the year ended January 2021, a gap of 18.2 points in Broadcom's favour; in the latest calendar-aligned quarter Broadcom is at 61.8% against NVIDIA's 68.0%, a gap of 6.2 points the other way.▪ On gross margin the same direction holds with less distance: Broadcom's segment went 70.0% (FY2023) to 69.5% (FQ2 FY2026) while NVIDIA's went 56.9% (year ended January 2023) to 74.9% in the latest quarter. Against Skyworks and Qorvo the advantage is widening on a shrinking base: 23 to 27 points of gross margin and 45 to 50 points of operating margin, with both peers in revenue decline. Against Marvell it is stable to widening: 17 and 48 points on the latest quarter, with Marvell's revenue growing 27.6% against Broadcom's 78.5%.

The advantage earns large excess returns today and is defensible for the programmes already contracted, and it is open to erosion as six buyers second-source. The one well-funded attempt to break it that has concluded, Apple's, succeeded.

Business-model analogues. The closest public comparables are Cadence Design Systems and Synopsys, whose advantage is also a silicon IP library plus a design methodology re-earned at each process node and amortized across many customers, and whose incumbency comes from a customer's unwillingness to re-qualify a proven flow. The analogue breaks on revenue form: electronic design automation is licensed per seat and recurs whether or not a chip ships, while Broadcom's ASIC revenue is per programme, so a lost socket removes the whole stream at once.▪ The second analogue is TSMC, which Tan named himself in April 2022, a franchise built on process continuity and multi-year commitments to a concentrated customer set. That one breaks on capital: TSMC's barrier is tens of billions of dollars of fabs a rival must physically duplicate, while Broadcom's is engineering methodology a well-resourced customer can hire toward, which is what MediaTek and Marvell are doing at Google now.

3.2 Infrastructure Software

This segment holds a demonstrated advantage over its customers and a much thinner one over the capital its owners committed to buy it.

Over 90% of VMware's 10,000 largest accounts bought VMware Cloud Foundation licences within two years of the acquisition, up from close to 3,000 accounts in June 2024. They did so while list prices rose by multiples: AT&T alleged a 1,050% increase on 75,000 virtual machines across roughly 8,600 servers and sued instead of migrating, then settled (techtarget.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Segment gross margin rose to 93.0% in FY2025 from 89.3%, and segment operating margin to 76.8% from 65.1%, while the absolute cost of revenue declined from $2,306m to $1,902m on 26% more revenue. A supplier that raises price several-fold and keeps nine tenths of its largest customers has priced against a switching cost those customers cannot pay to escape inside a renewal cycle.▪ The AT&T case measures that cost from the customer's own pleadings.

The return on what was paid is much lower. Broadcom paid roughly $127.0bn net of divestitures to assemble this segment: $5.2bn for Brocade after the $800m IP Networking sale, $20.1bn for CA including assumed bonds and net of Veracode, $10.7bn for the Symantec enterprise assets, and $91.0bn for VMware including assumed notes and net of the $3.5bn end-user computing sale. On that capital the segment produced FY2025 operating income of $20,765m before stock compensation and acquisition-intangible amortization. Deducting an estimated $3.0-4.2bn of segment stock compensation and taxing at 16% gives NOPAT of $13.9-14.9bn, a return of 11.0% to 11.8% on what was paid▪ [estimate: the only estimated input is the stock-compensation allocation, bracketed on revenue share and on operating-expense share]. The same calculation on the pre-VMware portfolio at FY2023 gives about 11.6%. Broadcom has bought an embedded software installed base four times since 2017, and the largest of the four earns the same rate as the three before it. Against a consolidated cost of capital near 8% — gross fixed-rate debt of $67.1bn at a 4.0% weighted coupon, a 3.4% after-tax cost, blended with an assumed 8.5% cost of equity on market weights — the segment earns roughly 300 basis points of excess return on the price paid.

The growth that produced the FY2025 numbers came from a conversion that is finished. Penetration of the top 10,000 accounts moved from roughly 3,000 accounts to over 90% across five quarters, and reported segment growth then went from +26% for FY2025 to +1.4% in FQ1 FY2026 and +8.8% in FQ2.▪ Tan described the next tier himself: "beyond the largest 10,000, are we seeing a lot of success? We are seeing some. But again, 2 reasons why we do not expect it to be necessarily successful" (FQ3 FY2025 call). Management then guided FQ3 FY2026 software revenue to roughly $8.9bn, up 31%, attributing the acceleration to CPU core counts shipping alongside AI accelerators. That driver is one quarter of guidance old and has not appeared in a reported result.

Virtualization has functional substitutes that a database format or a mainframe instruction set does not.▪ Gartner projects VMware's share of its market declining from 70% in 2024 to 40% in 2029, and a Rimini Street survey of 111 VMware customers in late 2024 found 36% had already switched and 98% were using, planning or considering alternatives, with 45% citing cost (networkworld.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Broadcom is also withdrawing from the parts of the base where those substitutes win: the VMware Cloud Service Provider programme closed in Europe in January 2026 with a 31 March deadline, leaving nine authorised providers in the UK and nineteen in the US, and CISPE filed a competition complaint with the European Commission on 19 March 2026 seeking interim measures (theregister.com and cispe.cloud, both accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. EMEA accounted for about $7.4bn, roughly 28%, of FY2025 software revenue [estimate: subscriptions-and-services revenue by region plus the regional split of upfront licence revenue in products, which leaves a $189m residual against segment revenue; the residual is Fibre Channel SAN hardware and other items the two disclosures split differently].

Testing the advantage against Nutanix, the closest pure-play comparable:

Measure FY2021 FY2023 FY2025 Latest quarter Direction
AVGO software segment operating margin 69.8% 73.8% 76.8% 78.7% Rising
Nutanix GAAP operating margin −47.5% −11.1% 6.8% 10.0% Rising faster
Gap, points 117 85 70 69 Narrowed 48 points in five years
AVGO software gross margin n/d 91.9% 93.0% 93.0% Rising
Nutanix gross margin 79.1% 82.2% 86.8% 86.9% Rising faster

Nutanix revenue growth +6.6% +17.8% +18.1% +10.0% —

The entire narrowing of the margin gap comes from Nutanix moving out of losses. The growth comparison is what changed: in the most recent reported quarters Nutanix grew faster than the segment it is attacking, on a base one tenth the size.▪ On return on the capital deployed the segment's 11.0-11.8% is close to IBM's 11.8%, below Cisco's 19.7% and well below Microsoft's 30.1%, and it has been flat for five years.

The advantage here is real and it is bounded by the renewal cycle: excess returns today, defensible through at least the FY2027-FY2028 renewals in the top 10,000 accounts, and eroding in the tail of the base where the price step has no offsetting value.▪ The mainframe and Fibre Channel portfolios inside the segment are more durable than VCF and smaller.

Business-model analogues. Roper Technologies and Constellation Software are the truest structural match: serial acquirers of embedded vertical software run for cash, with low organic growth and high margins funded by disciplined cost, buying an installed base instead of winning one.▪ The analogue breaks on concentration, because Roper and Constellation own hundreds of small niches and no single displacement threat resembles what Nutanix and the hyperscalers pose to vSphere. Oracle's database franchise is the closer analogue on pricing mechanism — an embedded standard repriced at renewal against customers whose migration cost exceeds the increase — and it breaks because Oracle built the standard and controls the data format, while a virtual machine can be converted.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

Broadcom's share of Google's TPU volume is the largest unresolved quantity in the forward model. Published estimates span 65% to 95% and no filing gives a figure, so what follows describes the structure of the market and not Broadcom's position inside its largest programme.▪

4.1 Data-centre silicon: structure and concentration

Annualizing each player's most recently reported quarter of data-centre silicon revenue, on each company's own disclosure and with the window named:

Player Latest quarter Window DC revenue ($m) Annualized ($m) Share YoY

Two qualifications apply. NVIDIA books rack-scale systems including memory, power and cooling content Broadcom never touches — Tan, asked directly on 3 June 2026 whether Broadcom sells racks: "No racks. It's chip." AMD's line includes server CPUs alongside accelerators. On a content-adjusted basis Broadcom's share of the underlying silicon is higher than 11.4%, and neither company discloses the split that would let anyone say how much higher.▪

Growth in Broadcom's segment costs gross margin and buys operating margin: consolidated gross margin is guided down to approximately 74% in FQ3 FY2026 from 77.1% on AI mix, while segment operating margin rose 460 basis points year on year to 61.8% because operating expense stayed at about 8% of revenue.

Who sets price. In merchant Ethernet switch silicon Broadcom is first on each generation and prices accordingly; it shipped the only 102 Tb/s switch for more than a year and taped out the 200 Tb/s part in FQ2 FY2026. In custom accelerators the customer owns the architecture, funds the programme and can re-bid each generation, so price is negotiated per generation.▪ What does show supplier power is order timing: AI bookings in FQ2 FY2026 exceeded $30bn against $10.8bn shipped, order visibility extended from 2027 to 2028 in a single quarter, and remaining performance obligations went from $33.3bn at 2 November 2025 to $45.0bn at 1 February 2026 to $164.6bn at 3 May 2026 on one contract. Customers are booking eighteen to twenty-four months of supply in advance.

4.2 Market sizing

Management's preferred unit is gigawatts of AI compute times Broadcom content per gigawatt, and both inputs come from earnings calls. Roughly 10 GW of shipments are planned for calendar 2027, back-half weighted, with "a lot more gigawatts" in 2028; content per gigawatt is given as $15-20bn, described as relatively stable within a generation and rising between generations. Ten gigawatts at $15-20bn is $150-200bn, against guidance of "in excess of $100 billion" for fiscal 2027.▪ Fiscal 2027 ends in October 2027 and the calendar ramp is back-half weighted, so part of a calendar-2027 shipment lands in fiscal 2028, which reconciles some of the gap and leaves the rest dependent on shipment timing nobody outside the company can observe. Joshua Buchalter put the arithmetic to Tan directly on the FQ2 FY2026 call and received an answer about content direction. Barclays reaches $150bn for calendar 2027 from the same two inputs and puts the Street's AI semiconductor expectation at roughly $120bn.

An independent sizing of Broadcom's share of new capacity: Morgan Stanley's internet team models hyperscaler capacity rising from roughly 30 GW in 2025 to roughly 120 GW by 2028, implying additions averaging roughly 30 GW a year, so Broadcom's 10 GW of planned 2027 shipments would be about a third of a year's additions [estimate: management's shipment guidance over a third-party capacity-addition forecast; both inputs are forecasts, so the result is directional].

Management's own market sizing has an eighteen-month half-life. At the FQ4 FY2024 call in December 2024 it put the fiscal-2027 serviceable market for accelerators and networking across its three then-customers at $60-90bn and said Broadcom expected a leading share of it. Eighteen months later the company guides its own fiscal-2027 AI revenue above $100bn.▪ The earlier figure was retired in June 2025 with "I'm not playing a SAM game here" and never restated.

Amazon's Trainium and Microsoft's Maia are the two largest internal accelerator programmes outside Google, and neither is a publicly identified Broadcom programme. Whether Broadcom is bidding on either is undisclosed, so the addressable customer set may be six or eight.

Those two figures are not a like-for-like split of one dollar — Arista's revenue is its own across all products and customers — and the allocation of an AI Ethernet switch dollar between silicon and system vendor is not established from them.

Bottom-up sizing of the private-cloud platform market: Broadcom's VMware at $18.8-19.8bn, Microsoft's entire on-premises Server products line at roughly $24bn growing about 1% [estimate: Microsoft discloses the $129,425m Server products and cloud services total and the two component growth rates of about 41% and about 1%, which solve to roughly $106bn of Azure and other cloud services and roughly $24bn of server products; only a minority of the server line is virtualization-attached and Microsoft does not split it], Nutanix at $2,538m, and IBM's Red Hat OpenShift above $2bn of ARR. Summing the identifiable virtualization-platform revenue gives roughly $30-38bn depending on how much of Microsoft's server line is attributed, of which Broadcom holds roughly 55-65% by revenue. Broadcom's workload share is lower than that revenue share, because its price per core is a multiple of the alternatives — Microsoft ships Hyper-V inside Windows Server and monetizes virtualization through the operating-system licence.▪

The pressure on VMware is structural and outside the accounts Broadcom serves. Nutanix's 3,220 net customer additions over twelve months equal about 1.1% of VMware's approximately 300,000-customer base on management's figure, and Broadcom has said the customers outside its top 10,000 produce much less value to it. The pool Nutanix, Hyper-V and Proxmox are converting is the roughly 290,000 accounts below that line, whose route to market Broadcom closed with the service-provider and white-label terminations.

4.7 Share counter-evidence, ranked by revenue exposed

  1. Google multi-sourcing. Tan conceded source diversity on 3 June 2026. Trade press reports Broadcom designing the training variant of the next TPU generation and MediaTek the inference variant, with Marvell on networking ASICs [web]. Morgan Stanley models Broadcom retaining roughly 80% of TPU volume; Macquarie, downgrading to Neutral on 4 June 2026 with a $437 target, models Broadcom's share of Google TPU revenue declining from roughly 95% in 2026 to 80% in 2027 and 65% in 2028 (finance.yahoo.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Applying Barclays' roughly $15bn per gigawatt to Morgan Stanley's estimate that 9 of Broadcom's roughly 14 GW of 2028 compute shipments are TPU puts the programme on the order of $110-140bn of 2028 revenue, so a 30-point share loss is roughly $33-42bn [estimate: two sell-side model assumptions multiplied; both are forecasts, so the range is wide and the midpoint is not usable].
  2. Customer in-sourcing, with a live precedent. Alchip, above. Broadcom's Item 1A names "their internal development of competing products or customer-owned tooling" as a customer-concentration risk, and the phrase entered the filings in the FQ1 FY2026 10-Q.
  3. Apple in wireless connectivity. The in-house combination chip displaces Broadcom content across iPhone, iPad and Mac. Broadcom's wireless line is roughly $7.5bn on the FY2024 build and comes almost entirely from that customer. Non-AI revenue has been flat at $4.0-4.6bn a quarter for eight quarters, so displacement is being offset by content elsewhere, and neither side of that offset is disclosed.
  4. NVIDIA in networking. Its data-centre networking revenue grew 199% to $14,800m in the quarter ended 26 April 2026 against Broadcom AI networking of roughly $4,300m growing roughly 145%. Broadcom management stated in FQ1 FY2026 that "we are clearly gaining share in networking." Both can hold on different denominators; on captured revenue NVIDIA gained $10.5bn more in the comparable quarter.
  5. Marvell as a fading threat. Its data-centre revenue grew 27% while Broadcom's AI revenue grew 143%, and it lost the Trainium 3 bake-off. It bought Celestial AI ($1.3bn cash plus 24.5m shares, closed 2 February 2026) and XConn ($280m plus 2.1m shares, closed 10 February 2026) to rebuild scale-up interconnect; neither contributed to that quarter.

Peer precedent for in-sourcing is thinner than it looks. Skyworks states in its FY2025 10-K that "we have lost content and sockets at our customers... including with our largest customer", and attributes the loss to not winning all the design competitions it entered, without naming customer silicon as the cause. Qorvo derives approximately 50% of FY2026 revenue from Apple against 47% in FY2025 and names "vertical integration by our customers" among its forward-looking risks.

5. Value chain and profit pools

No disclosure splits one dollar of end-customer AI spend across substrate, foundry, memory, packaging, silicon, system vendor and operator. What supports the claim that Broadcom captures the rack around the accelerator is the layer margins that follow and the served-market maps in Appendix A.

5.1 One dollar of Broadcom semiconductor revenue

Of every dollar of semiconductor segment revenue in FQ2 FY2026, 69.5 cents stayed as segment gross profit and 30.5 cents went to purchased wafers, memory, packaging, test, substrate, freight and Broadcom's own fab costs (10-Q FQ2 FY2026 segment note: revenue $15,009m, cost of revenue $4,573m). Infrastructure software has a different chain: revenue $7,178m, cost of revenue $505m, gross margin 93.0%, with no physical upstream to share with. Segment gross profit across the two divided by consolidated revenue reproduces the 77.1% consolidated gross margin management reported, so these figures reconcile to the call and not to the GAAP income statement, where consolidated gross margin was 69.5% after acquisition-intangible amortization in cost of revenue.

Migration on the same layers: Micron +63 points from 22% in FY2024, TSMC +16 points from 51.6% in 2021, Amkor +2 points and ASE +1 point, Broadcom's semiconductor segment −0.5 points from FY2023 with a further roughly 4 points implied by the FQ3 FY2026 guide, NVIDIA −4 points, Arista −2 points and Astera −1 point. Every input layer gained margin and every silicon and systems layer lost it or is guiding to lose it.▪ The two assembly-and-test companies attribute their gains to factory utilisation and not to price — Amkor's 10-Q says "primarily due to higher factory utilization driven by the increase in net sales" — so that layer is capturing volume.

Scale differs by an order of magnitude at the capital line. TSMC produced US$121,423m of CY2025 revenue on US$40,895m of capital expenditure, 33.7% of revenue, and guides 2026 to US$52-56bn. Broadcom produced $63,887m on $623m, 1.0%.

5.3 The binding constraint, and where it moved

The evidence supports memory first, customer-side power second, and foundry third.▪

Micron's FQ3 FY2026 10-Q states that "AI-driven memory and storage growth is outpacing industry supply... This has led to decisions on supply allocation that may impact certain customers and end markets." Its strategic customer agreements are structured as take-or-pay with binding volume commitments, and "the largest agreements generally have a ceiling price for existing products that approximates the market price in the second calendar quarter of 2026, and a floor price through the term." Micron expects those agreements, even at floor pricing, to yield gross margins well above its peak in any past cycle. Morgan Stanley's memory work puts DRAM pricing up 70% quarter on quarter in 1Q CY2026 and over 40% in 2Q, with at least another 25% expected in 3Q. Broadcom passes memory through at cost, which transfers the price move to the customer only where it re-prices; on fixed-price multi-generation agreements it does not.

Alphabet's FY2025 10-K names the customer-side constraint: "Our ability to scale our technical infrastructure is increasingly constrained by the availability of power, water, and land." Tan gives the same answer for why bookings run so far ahead of shipments. PJM's capacity auction for 2027/28 procured 145,777 MW, 6.6 GW below its reliability requirement, and average interconnection time in that market has risen from under two years in 2008 to over eight (introl.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Which specific sites, utilities and energization dates stand behind the roughly 10 GW planned for 2027 is not established anywhere, so power remains a management assertion supported by one market-level datapoint.

Foundry is where the filings and the calls disagree. Item 1A treats TSMC dependence — approximately 95% of contract-manufactured wafers in FY2025 — and five single-source materials suppliers as the operating risk, and notes that "TSMC has raised, and may in the future raise, their prices to manufacture our wafers." Management treats supply as secured and power as the limit. On the FQ2 FY2026 call Tim Arcuri asked whether Broadcom was "beginning to consider maybe using other foundries to add more optionality"; Tan answered on supply security and not on foundry diversification. Seven weeks later, on 25 July 2026, Samsung and Broadcom announced a non-binding memorandum of understanding covering more than $200bn of Samsung memory and foundry products through 2030, including HBM for next-generation accelerators, 2nm-and-below foundry and 2.3D/2.5D advanced packaging (news.samsung.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web, unverified — the release did not fetch directly, and the terms here come from a search summary]. JPMorgan estimates Samsung would supply 75-85% of Broadcom's HBM requirement with the purchase mix 90-95% memory and 5-10% foundry wafers, so the memorandum is primarily a memory arrangement.

5.4 Bargaining power at each interface

Upstream, Broadcom converted supplier power into a fixed obligation. The $128,110m of unconditional purchase commitments at 3 May 2026, against $132m at FY2025 year-end, is the price of the "supply is secured" claim, and its composition is undisclosed. TSMC's ten largest customers were 70%, 76% and 78% of its revenue in 2023, 2024 and 2025, so concentration on that side is rising too, and TSMC's High Performance Computing platform grew 48% year on year to 58% of revenue.

Downstream, three concentrations moved the same way in two quarters: the largest distributor from 32% of net revenue to 42%, the distributor channel from 48% to 56%, and the top five end customers from about 40% to about 45% for the half after 50% in FQ1. One customer accounted for 44% of net accounts receivable at 2 November 2025 against 18% a year earlier. The 10-Q's own list of distributor risks notes that "our distributors and other channel partners are generally not subject to minimum sales requirements or any obligation to market our products."

5.5 Customer-side economics

Customer 2026 capital expenditure Server and network depreciable life
Alphabet $80.6bn in H1 CY2026 against $39.6bn a year earlier six years
Meta $130-145bn guided for CY2026; $49.11bn of purchases in H1 5.5 years, extended from January 2025
Microsoft — six years

Alphabet funded the step with $20.5bn of share issuance, a $10.0bn private placement, $19.0bn of mandatory convertible preferred in June 2026, a $40.0bn at-the-market programme and $51.8bn of senior notes in the half, and holds $85.2bn of data-centre leases signed but not commenced. Meta issued $24.91bn of senior notes in May 2026.

Testing the return on a gigawatt: Broadcom's disclosed content is $15-20bn per gigawatt and Barclays models $15bn. Total infrastructure cost per gigawatt is roughly $42bn [estimate: Morgan Stanley models Alphabet capital expenditure of $375bn in CY2028 against roughly 9 GW of incremental capacity that year; this mixes a company-wide capex figure with one company's capacity addition, so treat it as an order of magnitude]. Broadcom's silicon is therefore roughly 36-48% of the total build, and that share includes memory it passes through. Annual ownership cost of a gigawatt is depreciation of roughly $5.2-7.0bn plus roughly $0.5bn of electricity [estimate: a six-to-eight-year blended life on $42bn; 1 GW at 85% load is 7.4 TWh a year at $0.07/kWh], so a 10% pre-tax return needs roughly $10-12bn of revenue per gigawatt-year before staff, networking and site costs. At Morgan Stanley's estimate of roughly 14 GW of Broadcom-supplied compute in CY2028, running that fleet at a 10% return requires roughly $140-170bn a year of revenue from Broadcom-supplied capacity alone. That revenue has to come from six customers, two of which are private, pre-profit and being financed into their compute by the vehicle Broadcom backstops.

5.6 The financing structures inside the chain

The FQ2 FY2026 10-Q's subsequent-events note discloses the arrangement in full: "On June 8, 2026, we arranged for an investor partner to take on certain agreements to purchase AI racks based on custom AI accelerators designed by us and the related lease agreements with a customer that enable access to compute capacity. In connection with the arrangement, we entered into a backstop agreement with the investor partner for the customer's lease obligations over 5-year terms. The backstop will increase over time as the AI racks are deployed and decrease as the customer makes payments on its lease obligations, with a maximum exposure of $29 billion." Part II Item 5 of the same filing names Apollo as the investor partner; Note 11 calls it "an investor partner". Three facts follow from the wording: Broadcom held agreements to purchase AI racks and the customer lease agreements, and transferred them; it retains the customer credit risk to a $29bn maximum; and its remedy on default is to assume the lease or sell used custom accelerators into a market of the same handful of buyers.

Apollo's own release of 9 June 2026 describes a $35bn first tranche of a platform designed for more than 20 GW of compute capacity through 2028, with Wells Fargo as global coordinator on the first tranche and Goldman Sachs, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley as joint placement agents on the second (ir.apollo.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Trade reporting describes the Broadcom obligation as a deficiency guarantee on residual value covering the senior notes, entered to achieve lower borrowing costs for the vehicle (capacityglobal.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web].

The risk-factor language escalated across the same three filings. The FY2025 10-K described customers "seeking to lease AI racks or systems based on our XPUs instead of purchasing, as well as alternative financings for such leases". The FQ1 FY2026 10-Q added that "such arrangements may impose financial obligations, including guarantees, upon us". The FQ2 FY2026 10-Q states that customers are "requiring us to purchase and then lease to them full AI racks or systems" and that "such arrangements have and may impose financial obligations, including backstops or guarantees, upon us."

6. Secular and industry trends

Broadcom's revenue responds to three demand systems, and the semiconductor segment contains two of them whose realized growth rates differ by roughly 175 percentage points in the current fiscal year.

Demand system FY2025 revenue Management's stated driver Ultimate exposure
AI semiconductors $20,190m Gigawatts of compute committed Capital spending and financing capacity at six named buyers
Non-AI semiconductors ~$16,668m "Cyclical recovery" Handset unit shipments (Apple-weighted), broadband access capex, enterprise IT budgets
Infrastructure software $27,029m VCF adoption and ARR Price realized on an existing installed base

6.1 Growth attribution against the realized record

Against Broadcom's own ultimate volume driver. The non-AI half of the semiconductor segment has not grown in six years: above $16,570m in FY2019 and $16,668m in FY2025. Every dollar of semiconductor growth since FY2019 came from the AI line.▪ Of the roughly $40bn FY2026 revenue increment, approximately $36bn is AI semiconductors, approximately $3bn is infrastructure software, and approximately $0.9bn is non-AI. One line item, sold to six customers, disclosed only on earnings calls, supplies 90% of the growth.▪

Against industry dollars. The WSTS Spring 2026 forecast, released 2 June 2026, puts the total world semiconductor market at $795,640m in 2025, +26.2%, with Logic at $299,547m, +38.8%, and Memory at $230,042m, +39.0% (wsts.org, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Broadcom's semiconductor products fall mostly into Logic, with filters in Analog and Discrete and lasers and optocouplers in Optoelectronics. In calendar 2025, the best year the semiconductor industry has had, Broadcom's semiconductor segment grew 22.4% while the Logic category grew 38.8%, so Broadcom's implied share of Logic went from 13.9% to 12.3%.▪ The share gain is entirely in the guide: FY2026 requires the segment to roughly double while Logic grows 37%. The ratio is above the true share because part of the segment falls in other categories and Logic is dominated by NVIDIA, so the direction is what matters. Broadcom's non-AI half against its own categories in calendar 2025: Analog +8.7%, Discrete −1.0%, Optoelectronics +4.7%, Sensors +10.4%, against non-AI at roughly −7%.

Against a peer growth cohort split by exposure.

Company Period ≈ CY2025 Revenue YoY Cohort
Credo FY ended May 2026 ~$1,335m +206% AI interconnect
Astera Labs CY2025 $832m +110% AI interconnect
AVGO AI semiconductors FY2025 $20,190m +65% AI silicon
NVIDIA FY ended Jan 2026 $215,938m +65% AI silicon
Marvell FY ended Jan 2026 ~$8,200m +42% AI silicon

AVGO semiconductor segment FY2025 $36,858m +22% blended
Qualcomm FY ended Sep 2025 $44,284m +14% handset and edge
Cisco FY ended Jul 2025 $56,654m +5% enterprise networking
