Qorvo ≈CY2025 $3,672m ~flat RF handset
AVGO non-AI semiconductors FY2025 ~$16,668m −7% handset, broadband, storage

Two things follow. Broadcom's AI line grew at exactly NVIDIA's total rate in the calendar-2025 window, 65% against 65%, so on realized numbers the custom-silicon architecture took no share from the merchant GPU in the year it was supposed to.▪ And Broadcom's non-AI line grew slower than every peer in the handset and enterprise cohort, including the two RF pure-plays whose end market is the same one. Broadcom grew like the AI cohort in one half and worse than the volume cohort in the other. Over the same period its lead over the merchant ASIC houses widened from 3.3x to 5.9x Marvell's data-centre revenue. Both are true on their own denominators: Broadcom is pulling away from the other custom-ASIC houses and is not taking share from the accelerator vendor or from the Logic category as a whole.

6.2 Cyclical against secular

The non-AI half is three years into a decline with no trough recovery. Peak to current is $24,382m (FY2023) to roughly $16,668m (FY2025), a decline of 32%, with FY2026 tracking about $17.6bn, still 28% below the peak. The FY2020 low of roughly $16.4bn and the FY2025 level are the same business five years apart. The first quantitative support for the recovery claim arrived in FQ2 FY2026: bookings above $6bn against roughly $4.2bn of revenue, and FQ3 guided to $4.5bn, up 12% year on year, the first double-digit non-AI growth rate since the downturn began. Working against it, IDC forecasts worldwide smartphone shipments down 13.9% in 2026 to 1.09bn units, the steepest annual contraction on record, attributing it to the memory shortage raising device bills of material and to Apple's base iPhone being delayed to early 2027 (idc.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. The AI buildout is squeezing the end market that funds Broadcom's largest non-AI line.

The AI half shows peak-cycle markers.

Marker FQ4 FY2025 FQ1 FY2026 FQ2 FY2026
AI semiconductor revenue $6.5bn $8.4bn $10.8bn
AI year-on-year growth +74% +106% +143%
AI bookings in the quarter — — over $30bn
Implied AI book-to-bill — — ~2.8x
Remaining performance obligations $33.3bn $45.0bn $164.6bn
RPO expected within twelve months 35% 33% 30%
Days of inventory on hand 58 68 86
Consolidated gross margin 77.9% 77.0% 77.1%, guided ~74% for FQ3

Accelerating year-on-year growth, a book-to-bill near three, inventory days rising 28 in two quarters, and remaining performance obligations growing 3.7x in one quarter on a single contract describe a demand pull-forward.▪ Management's own explanation is that customers order eighteen to twenty-four months ahead because they must sequence power and memory, and that visibility now runs to 2028. Long-dated orders raise reported backlog and simultaneously raise the risk that the backlog stretches instead of converting.

Almost none of the FY2026 growth comes from the semiconductor cycle. If the order book converts on schedule the trend is secular for at least three years, because 2027 shipments are contracted and 2028 visibility exists. If it stretches, there is no second source of growth: non-AI is flat and software is a fixed installed base being repriced.

6.3 What changes the slope

Raising it: content per accelerator rising a generation at a time as packages add memory stacks, embedded CPU cores and SRAM; Google beginning to sell TPU systems for deployment in customers' own data centres, with Meta reported to have signed a multibillion-dollar agreement in February 2026 to access them (finance.yahoo.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web], which decouples Broadcom's TPU volume from Google's own capital spending; Ethernet displacing InfiniBand and contesting NVLink; and single-site power ceilings forcing multi-site training, which is what the Jericho deep-buffer line sells into.

Lowering it: MediaTek at Google, with a doubled 2026 AI ASIC revenue target of about $2bn and a stated 10-15% market share ambition (trendforce.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web], which at Broadcom's guided FY2026 accelerator revenue of roughly $34bn would represent $3.4-5.1bn of displaced revenue at that share [estimate]; memory cost, with WSTS forecasting the memory market up 249.5% in 2026; customer-side power and interconnection queues; handset units down 13.9%; the Section 232 semiconductor tariff of 25% from January 2026, currently narrow under its data-centre and research exemptions with a review that could widen it (whitecase.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]; and China at 17% of FY2025 net revenue by shipment location, down from 20%, with the company stating end demand dependent on China is substantially smaller.

Power scarcity is closer to neutral for Broadcom than for its customers, because it both defers conversion and creates product demand: interconnection queues delay gigawatt deployment and simultaneously force training and inference across multiple sites, which is the Jericho use case. The exposure is timing until a customer cancels instead of rescheduling.

7. Critical points

1. Broadcom signed a $128,110m supplier obligation and a $164.6bn customer obligation in the same quarter, and the filings connect neither to the other. Unconditional, non-cancelable purchase commitments went from $54m at 1 February 2026 to $128,110m at 3 May 2026, on the schedule set out in Section 12. Remaining performance obligations went from $45.0bn to $164.6bn over the same quarter, which the 10-Q attributes to "a long-term contract for custom AI accelerators entered in the fiscal quarter ended May 3, 2026". If both attach to the same programme, $128.1bn of purchases against $164.6bn of contracted revenue implies a lifetime gross margin near 22% against a 69.5% segment gross margin today. If they do not, then $128.1bn of binding purchases stands against revenue that is not contracted as the filing defines contracted. Neither the call nor the management discussion addresses the schedule.

2. The FQ3 FY2026 gross-margin guide breaks the semiconductor segment's own margin for the first time in the AI era, and mix explains a sixth of it. Holding both segments at their FQ2 FY2026 gross margins of 69.5% and 93.0% and applying the guided revenue mix of roughly $20.5bn and $8.9bn produces a consolidated 76.6%. The guide is approximately 74%. Segment mix accounts for 0.5 of the 3.1-point decline▪; the other 2.6 points, about $776m of gross profit in one quarter, requires the semiconductor segment's own gross margin near 66%, roughly 380 basis points below FQ2 [estimate: solving $29,400m × 0.74 = $8,900m × 0.93 + $20,500m × g; the answer ranges 65-67% across software margins of 92-93% and a consolidated guide of 74.0-74.5%]. Two candidates fit: networking falling back from 40% toward 30% of AI revenue, and memory, substrate and packaging content per accelerator stepping up at a pass-through markup. FQ3 reports on 2 September 2026.

3. Roughly four-fifths of the FY2026 accelerator revenue increase is price per unit. Section 1.2 sets that split at about 2.7x on revenue against about 1.1-1.3x on units, so most of the headline AI growth rate is content inflation flowing through the revenue line [estimate: the unit count comes from third-party estimates and the price share of the increase ranges from about 75% to 92% across the bounds]. Of the FY2026 price per unit, $2,500-3,300 is memory bought at contract price from three suppliers. Growth sourced that way shows up in gross margin before it shows up in unit demand, which is what point 2 describes.

4. The AI half of the semiconductor segment appears to earn a higher gross margin than the non-AI half, which runs against how both management and consensus describe custom accelerators. Two two-equation solves on filed segment revenue and filed segment cost of revenue, over period pairs in which the mix moved sharply, converge: FY2024 against FY2025 gives AI 70.5% and non-AI 65.3%; FQ2 FY2025 against FQ2 FY2026 gives 70.7% and 66.4%.▪ A third solve over consecutive FY2026 quarters, where the mix barely moved, is ill-conditioned and gives 75.6% and 54.0%; it agrees on the direction and not the size of the gap. On the two stable solves the AI half runs roughly 400-500 basis points above the non-AI half, which on FQ2 AI revenue of $10,800m is roughly $450-550m of quarterly gross profit [estimate: bounds from the two well-conditioned solves; the estimate assumes per-line margins were stable within each period pair, and the networking mix did move from 40% to 40% via 35% across the annual pair]. Realized segment gross margin corroborates the direction, rising from 68.1% in FY2025 to 69.5% in FQ2 FY2026 while AI went from 55% to 72% of the segment. The "AI is dilutive" framing survives because management compares AI against the 93% software segment, where it is trivially true, and because consolidated gross margin does decline for reasons of segment mix.

5. Non-AI semiconductors are not a cyclical trough waiting to recover; they are three years into a decline management has twice called wrong. Revenue was $24.4bn in FY2023, $17.9bn in FY2024, $16.7bn in FY2025 and is tracking about $17.6bn in FY2026 — 28% below FY2023 three years on, and below the $17.8bn management declared as the cyclical bottom in December 2024 while forecasting mid-single-digit growth from that level. Over FY2023-FY2025 this half subtracted $7.7bn, offsetting 47% of what AI added. It is now roughly 24% of the segment and falling as a share every quarter, so the diversification argument covers less than a quarter of the segment.

6. The software segment earns roughly 11% on what was paid for it against a 76.8% reported margin, and the growth that produced that margin is finished. The 11.0-11.8% return on the $127.0bn paid, derived in Section 3.2, stands against a consolidated return on invested capital of 16.9% and a cost of capital near 8%. VCF penetration of the top 10,000 accounts went from roughly 3,000 accounts to over 90% in five quarters and reported growth then went to +1.4%. Management's own view of the next tier is that it does not expect the same result. The FQ3 FY2026 guide of +31% depends on a mechanism — CPU core counts shipping alongside AI accelerators — that has appeared in one quarter of guidance and no reported result.

7. Three concentrations moved together and one of them is a credit exposure. The largest distributor went from 32% of net revenue to 42%, the distributor channel from 48% to 56%, and one customer from 18% to 44% of net accounts receivable. That customer is unnamed in every filing from FQ2 FY2024 onward. At $10,830m of receivables on 3 May 2026, a comparable share would be roughly $4.8bn of exposure to one intermediary [estimate: the FY2025 receivable-concentration percentage applied to the current balance; the percentage is not restated quarterly, so treat as an order of magnitude]. Section 18 sets out how one AI customer's deferral moves revenue, receivable ageing, inventory and the backstop together.

8. Management's disclosure horizon is inverted by auditability. Broadcom has not guided full-year consolidated revenue since FY2024 and guides the audited consolidated figure one quarter ahead. It guides AI semiconductor revenue — which appears in no 10-K or 10-Q and has no published definition — for the full current fiscal year, the next fiscal year, and qualitatively for the year after. Consolidated backlog was headlined at $110bn in September 2025 and $162bn in December 2025 and has not been given since; when an analyst asked directly on 3 June 2026 whether the eighteen-month AI backlog now stood at $200bn or better, Tan answered the revenue parts of the question. The replacement disclosure is a single-quarter bookings figure.

9. The company is generating more cash than its stated uses can absorb and has no announced destination for it. The base case in Section 17 produces $702,235m of cumulative free cash flow over FY2026-FY2032 against $306,595m of dividends on the stated policy and $12,527m of debt maturing through FY2029. The historical answer has been another software installed base at an 11% return, and that programme has been dormant since April 2024, the longest gap since FY2017. Repurchases have never reduced the share count: $50,627m of open-market and tax-withholding repurchase across ten years against a diluted count 26.7% higher than FY2016.

10. Broadcom's realized AI growth matched NVIDIA's total growth in calendar 2025 and underperformed the Logic category. 65% against 65%, with the semiconductor segment at 22.4% against Logic at 38.8%, so implied Logic share went from 13.9% to 12.3%. Every point of the claimed share gain is in the FY2026 and FY2027 guide. The opposite comparison holds at the same time — Broadcom is pulling away from Marvell, GUC and Alchip — because the two use different denominators.

8. Management claim pressure tests

Supply is secured through 2028. Tan, 4 March 2026: "we have fully secured capacity of these components for '26 through '28", with Charlie Kawwas adding "We're probably the first one to secure that up to '28 or beyond." The 10-Q for the quarter that had ended a month earlier showed $54m of unconditional purchase commitments in total. Whatever "fully secured" described on that date, it was not an enforceable, legally binding obligation; it became one during the following quarter, at $128,110m. On 3 June 2026 the stated horizon moved back: "we have been able to secure supply of the types you mentioned about 4 needs, '26, '27. Working on '28 and '29 right now." The claim is now supported by a balance-sheet commitment whose counterparties, products and price basis are undisclosed, and the horizon it covers moved in one quarter from three years to two.

AI mix does not compress gross margin. Three positions in three consecutive quarters. Spears, 11 December 2025: "we'll be passing through more components that are not ours... And so those gross margins will be lower." Tan, 4 March 2026, to an analyst sizing rack gross margin at 45-50% and modelling a 500-basis-point consolidated decline: "Hate to tell you that you must be a bit hallucinated. Our gross margin is solidly at the number Kirsten report. We will not be affected." Spears on the same call: "the impact relative to our overall mix is actually not going to be substantial at all. So I wouldn't worry about it." The FY2025 10-K, filed in December 2025 and repeated in the FQ1 FY2026 10-Q, states that the sale or leasing of AI racks "will likely increase our operating margin but compress or lower future gross margin, which would adversely impact our stock price." On 3 June 2026 Spears guided consolidated gross margin down 310 basis points to approximately 74% and added: "We highly recommend that investors model semiconductor and infrastructure software margins separately." Segment mix explains 0.5 of the 3.1 points. In the same Q&A Spears also acknowledged the within-segment source directly — "Within semiconductors, we've always said our ASICs, TPUs... has lower margins" — so the two attributions coexist in one call.

No racks; it is a chip business. Tan, 11 December 2025, on the Anthropic order: "it's a system sale... we believe it begins to make sense to do it as a system sale and be responsible, but be fully responsible for the entire system or rack, as you call it." Tan and Spears, 3 June 2026: "No racks. It's chip." / "Chip business only." / "We own chips." The FQ2 FY2026 10-Q risk factors, covering the quarter that ended a month before that call, state that customers are "requiring us to purchase and then lease to them full AI racks or systems based on our XPUs instead of purchasing these chips or racks directly." The 10-Q's subsequent-events note describes rack purchase agreements and customer lease agreements Broadcom held and transferred. The delivery model changed between December 2025 and June 2026, which changes revenue per gigawatt, gross margin and working capital, and no filing reconciles the two descriptions.

The Anthropic arrangement is not a Broadcom backstop. Asked on 3 June 2026 whether the transaction was backstopped by Broadcom chips, Tan corrected the premise: "I have to correct you on that... it wasn't backstop in that sense. We were the one providing the chips... We were the one providing the compute capacity." Five days later, on 8 June 2026, Broadcom entered a backstop agreement covering a customer's five-year lease obligations with a maximum exposure of $29bn, disclosed in the 10-Q filed on 9 June. Apollo's release of 9 June identifies the platform and the frontier-lab lessee. The question and the agreement address different objects — the analyst asked about chips, the agreement covers lease obligations — and the sequencing is five days.

Content per gigawatt is $15-20bn and relatively stable. Management also guides roughly 10 GW of shipments in 2027 against AI revenue "in excess of $100 billion", which implies about $10bn per gigawatt. Two analysts put the discrepancy directly to Tan, on the FQ1 and FQ2 FY2026 calls, and neither received a reconciliation; his FQ1 answer was "The dollars per gigawatt is varies, sometimes quite dramatically." The likely explanation is scope: the $15-20bn figure came from system sales — the two Anthropic orders were $10bn and $11bn for roughly 1 GW each, and Tan called that a system sale — while the FY2027 guide is chip-only after the June 2026 clarification. If so the two numbers measure different things and no filing says so. Neither version has been published in a filing, and the difference between them is worth $50-100bn of FY2027 revenue.

AI networking settles near 30% of AI revenue. Five disclosed observations: 40% (FQ1 FY2025), 40% (FQ2 FY2025), 35% (FQ3 FY2025), 33% (FQ1 FY2026), almost 40% (FQ2 FY2026), averaging about 38% with a minimum of 33%. Tan on 3 June 2026: "Not the first time I indicated that the more expected percentage as a share of total AI revenue for networking would be closer to around 30%." Management has now been wrong on this three times in the same direction. The error has run in Broadcom's favour on margin each time, because networking is the richer half, where the residual solve puts gross margin at 75-80% against 64-68% for accelerators.▪ The FQ3 FY2026 gross-margin guide assumes the pattern does not repeat.

Non-AI bottomed at $17.8bn in FY2024 and recovers at mid-single digits. Stated 12 December 2024. FY2025 delivered about $16.7bn and FY2026 is tracking about $17.6bn. Every quarterly non-AI guide in that span was hit; the multi-year framework was not.

FY2025 growth was organic. Management described consolidated FY2025 growth of 24% as organic on the FQ4 FY2025 call. In the same year, software's revenue rose $5,551m, of which $3,199m came from a larger upfront-recognized licence component ($7,800m against $4,601m), and $4,601m of FY2024 revenue and $1,058m of FY2023 revenue were reclassified between products and subscriptions to conform to the new presentation. Upfront recognition applies to arrangements without termination-for-convenience rights, so the year-to-year figure follows contract terms and renewal timing.

Software backlog was $73bn at FY2025 year-end, against $49bn a year earlier. Backlog rose $24bn in a year in which the segment recognized $27,029m of revenue, while the two quarters of that year in which total contract value was disclosed were "over $8.4 billion" (FQ3 FY2025) and "exceeded $10.4 billion" (FQ4 FY2025). Broadcom has published no definition of backlog that reconciles those series to each other or to the filed remaining performance obligations of $33.3bn for both segments on the same date. Management stopped citing consolidated backlog after December 2025, and total contract value was disclosed for FQ3 FY2025, FQ4 FY2025 and FQ1 FY2026 and not for FQ2 FY2026.

Customer-owned tooling will not compete for many years. Tan, 11 December 2025: "I see that as this concept of customer tooling is an overblown hypothesis, which frankly, I don't think will happen." 4 March 2026: "we will not see competition in COT for many years to come. It will come eventually, but we're still a long way off." 3 June 2026: "we fully expect that there will be some diversity of sources for them." Over the same three quarters "customer-owned tooling" entered Item 1A, appearing in the FQ1 FY2026 10-Q and in no earlier Broadcom filing.

The 2018 pattern is the precedent for how management handles a conceded share loss. On the FQ3 FY2018 call, on losing RF content at the largest customer: "from time to time, not that often but time to time, the same technology platform used by our customer may extend beyond one generation... we believe we are very well positioned to win back the platform." On 3 June 2026, on Google: the concession, then "our commitment from them is a very substantial dollar mark." In both cases the share point was conceded and the answer pointed to the next generation. Across the 46 quarterly calls in the record the clearest acknowledgment of an adverse outcome remains the blocked Qualcomm bid, attributed to a government order, and the nearest admission of a limitation is FQ3 FY2024 on the sequencing of accelerator against networking deployment: "we don't really predict very well, nor understand completely except in hindsight."

Five inflections define the record.

Broadcom Corporation, February 2016. Avago paid $35,706m for a company larger than itself, took its name and moved from a $6.8bn RF-and-storage supplier to a $13bn diversified group. It took three fiscal years for GAAP operating margin to return to the pre-deal level while revenue tripled, because acquisition-intangible amortization ran through the income statement; free cash flow, which the amortization does not touch, grew 207% between FY2016 and FY2018. The deal established the pattern: pay a full price for scale, accept years of depressed GAAP earnings, and divest alongside acquiring.

Qualcomm blocked, then CA bought, March to November 2018. The Qualcomm outcome was forced; the CA response was chosen within four months and against the market, redeploying the same borrowing capacity into an unrelated asset class. Semiconductor revenue declined 8.5% in FY2019 while software revenue grew 190%. Consolidated gross margin has risen in seven of the eight years since, from 51.5% to 67.8%, and software has been the higher-margin half every year it has existed. The acquisition test the company applies came from the same call: buy where the core business is "not so focused on or neglected in many ways, and instead the bright, shiny objects get focused on," then "pull them back to their roots."

The June 2019 guidance cut. Broadcom cut FY2019 revenue from $24.5bn to $22.5bn and semiconductor revenue from $19.5bn to $17.5bn, and actual FY2019 revenue was $22,597m with semiconductor at $17,441m, so the revised guide held. In the same prepared remarks that cut revenue 8%, the CFO raised the non-GAAP operating margin guide about 150 basis points to about 52.5%, held the dividend and restated an $8bn repurchase commitment. R&D rose from $3,768m to $4,696m in the same year and capital expenditure came in at $432m, the second-lowest of the decade. Asked how much of the $2bn was Huawei, Tan disclosed that Huawei had been "about $900 million of revenues for this company by itself" the prior year, so roughly 55% of the cut was elsewhere.

VMware, announced May 2022, closed November 2023. Because the shares rose sharply between announcement and close, the recorded consideration was $30,800m of cash plus 544 million split-adjusted shares at a fair value of $53,400m, about 38% above the announced headline. FY2024 revenue grew 44% while GAAP operating income declined from $16,207m to $13,463m and net income from $14,082m to $5,895m, including the only quarterly loss in the record. Headcount went from about 20,000 to about 37,000 at close and back to about 33,000 within two years.

Custom AI silicon, FY2023 to FY2026. A franchise below 5% of semiconductor revenue until 2022 became the majority of the company. This was not planned: the capability was built over a decade for a different purpose and the demand arrived on top of it. What management did choose was disclosure and capacity — the reporting frame changed to AI against non-AI in December 2024, and the supply commitments followed in 2026. The company monetised the windfall through the income statement: revenue grew 78% between FY2023 and FY2025 while capital expenditure went from $452m to $623m. The counterpart is working capital, where receivables and inventory together grew from $9,415m at FY2025 year-end to $15,158m at 3 May 2026.

What the record shows about behaviour. Under a demand shock, margin and capital return are defended before volume, and engineering is not cut. Under competitive attack the response is a cadence argument: concede the share point, point to the next generation. Windfalls go to dividends and debt, and the buyback is residual — nil in FY2016, FY2017, FY2020 and FY2021, then $7,850m in a single quarter in FQ1 FY2026. Acquisitions follow a fixed sequence: buy an under-managed installed base, halve the spending, convert the licence terms, sell what does not fit, deleverage. And disclosure narrows as concentration widens: named foundries went from six in FY2018 to one in FY2020, named competitors from 56 in FY2024 to zero in FY2025, and Apple was named as a revenue concentration for six consecutive years, at 15% to 25% of net revenue, and removed from the FY2024 filing.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Who runs the company

Four people were the entire executive officer roster for fiscal 2025: Hock Tan (President and CEO since March 2006, age 74, also a director of Meta Platforms), Kirsten Spears (CFO), Mark Brazeal (Chief Legal and Corporate Affairs Officer) and Charlie Kawwas (President, Semiconductor Solutions Group). Two changes since. Amie Thuener became CFO on 12 June 2026, hired from Alphabet where she was corporate controller and chief accounting officer from 2018 (cfodive.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]; Alphabet is Broadcom's largest custom-accelerator customer. Ram Velaga, who ran the Core Switching Group and was the public architect of the Ethernet position through the 2024 investor meeting, became President of the Infrastructure Software Group in January 2026 and appears as an executive officer in Form 4 filings from March 2026. Broadcom stopped publishing its divisional general-manager roster between the December 2025 and March 2026 investor decks [deck: company overview series].

The board after the April 2026 meeting has eight members, seven classified independent, including Henry Samueli as Chairman. Harry You chairs the Compensation Committee. Thomas Krause, CFO and then President of the software group, resigned in July 2022 and forfeited all unvested equity with no severance.

10.2 What management is paid for

Cash pay is small and frozen. Tan's salary has been $1,200,000 since 2020 and he takes no annual bonus; the independent directors "do not intend to provide Mr. Tan with annual cash incentive opportunities under the APB Plan through fiscal 2027". The annual bonus for the other officers is set by two corporate goals weighted equally, revenue and adjusted non-GAAP operating margin, both of which exceeded their maximum in fiscal 2025 and were capped.

The margin metric is measured after adding back the pay. The 2026 proxy bridges FY2025 GAAP operating income of $25,484m to the plan measure by adding $8,062m of acquisition-intangible amortization, $7,568m of stock-based compensation, $667m of restructuring, $216m of acquisition costs and $1,379m of accrued bonus, reaching $43,376m, or 68.0% of revenue against a GAAP operating margin of 39.9%. Granting more equity does not reduce measured attainment, and the bonus accrual is added back before the bonus is calculated. In the other direction, the committee excluded $303m of unanticipated VMware revenue from the fiscal 2024 revenue measure, which reduced attainment.

Long-term incentives are front-loaded multi-year grants and no options have been granted since 2015. Two awards define the structure:

Award Granted Size Measure Status
2023 Tan PSU 31 Oct 2022 up to 10,000,000 post-split shares; grant-date fair value of the maximum $160,540,000 20-day average close of $82.50, $95.00 and $112.50 post-split during an Earning Period from 31 Oct 2025 to 31 Oct 2027; one third per hurdle, no interpolation The close on 31 October 2025, the first day of the Earning Period, was $369.63, 3.3x the top hurdle. All three were satisfied at the moment the period opened. The proxy values full acceleration at $3,696,300,000
2025 Tan PSU 3 Sep 2025 target 610,521 shares, maximum 1,831,563 (300%); grant-date fair value at target $202,351,080 Highest four-consecutive-quarter AI Revenue between the start of fiscal 2028 and the end of fiscal 2030: $60bn threshold (0%), $90bn target (100%), $105bn stretch (200%), $120bn maximum (300%) Vests on the last day of fiscal 2030

The 2025 award's measure is defined in the proxy as revenue from products "used or expected to be used by our customers for AI enablement, including but not limited to our custom AI accelerators, XPUs, ASICs, networking and connectivity solutions, and AI racks or systems based on our XPUs." The proxy calls the hurdles "formidable" and anchors the threshold to "more than three times the $20 billion of fiscal 2025 AI Revenue that was forecasted."

Against that framing, the hurdles are close to what the company already guides. FQ3 FY2026 AI semiconductor revenue is guided to $16bn, an annualized $64bn, which exceeds the $60bn threshold two full fiscal years before the performance period opens. Fiscal 2027 AI revenue is guided "in excess of $100 billion", above the $90bn target and within 5% of the $105bn stretch. Applying an AI share of 45-65% to Bloomberg's consensus fiscal-2028 revenue of $229,361m gives $103-149bn in the first year of the three-year measurement window [estimate: consensus revenue times an assumed AI mix bracketing the 53% implied by FY2026 guidance], with the midpoint at the $120bn maximum. For the award to pay nothing, AI revenue would have to fall roughly 40% below its guided fiscal-2027 level and stay there for three years.

The metric has no margin, capital or per-share condition, and it counts pass-through content. Gross margin is guided down to about 74% for FQ3 FY2026 on AI mix, and the definition includes racks and systems, whose bought-in memory is revenue at low incremental margin. At the $120bn maximum, a 25-point difference between a chip mix and a system mix is roughly $30bn of gross profit, and none of it changes the payout. Neither the bonus plan nor either CEO award contains a per-share, return-on-capital or free-cash-flow measure; the only relative benchmark anywhere in the programme applies to the two lowest-paid officers, whose performance units are measured on total shareholder return against the S&P 500.

Fiscal 2025 pay: Tan $205,278,006 (of which $202,351,080 is the 2025 award and $1,693,020 is residential and personal security), Spears $28,164,046, Brazeal $28,619,011, Kawwas $2,115,626. The CEO pay ratio is 543 to 1 on the reported figure and 93 to 1 on the supplemental basis Broadcom also publishes, which replaces the 2025 award with one fifth of the 2023 award. Compensation Actually Paid to the CEO under the pay-versus-performance rules totals $4,320m over five years against cumulative net income of $61,334m, 7.0%, and 0.28% of the $1.56tn increase in market capitalization from the end of fiscal 2020 to the end of fiscal 2025.

On a covered termination outside a change of control at fiscal 2025 year-end, Tan's cash package is $1,200,000 of salary plus $17,682 of health continuation against equity acceleration of $3,696,300,000; Kawwas's is $901,250 of cash against $1,108,890,000 of equity. No change-in-control payment is single-trigger on the cash, and the cash is a small share of what leaves with the executive.

Shareholders have responded to the grant cycle. Say-on-pay support: about 80% in 2022, 32% in 2023, 61% in 2024, 92% in 2025 and 66.4% in 2026, falling in the years after a large grant and recovering in the year the CEO receives nothing. At the April 2026 meeting the three Compensation Committee members drew the three largest opposition votes, with the chair at 74.0% support against 99.7% for Tan himself.

10.3 Insider ownership

Tan's beneficial ownership went from 1,844,746 shares at the February 2025 record date to 908,474 at the February 2026 record date, a reduction of 936,272 shares or 50.8%. The chain reconciles to Form 4 sales of 100,000 shares on 23 December 2025 at $345.65 and 70,000 on 6 January 2026 at $347.30 (secform4.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]; aggregator reports record further sales in September and December 2025 [web, unverified]. Proceeds on the full reduction are roughly $310m [estimate: 936,272 shares at an assumed $335 average, the midpoint of the $326-347 range on the disclosed Form 4 sales; range $305-325m]. The ownership guideline of 6x a $1,200,000 salary is about 18,000 shares, so it is met roughly fifty times over and constrains nothing; Tan's economic exposure is concentrated in the unvested 2023 award. Henry Samueli holds 85,559,569 shares, 1.8% of the company, of which 16,175,000 are pledged under a board-approved exception. Excluding him, the entire board and management own under 0.1%.

As a share of the $136,684m of operating cash flow: acquisitions net of divestitures 44.9%, dividends 41.8%, open-market repurchase 25.7%, shares withheld for employee taxes 11.3%, capital expenditure 4.3%. The uses sum to 128% of operating cash flow; net debt issuance, preferred and common issuance and divestiture proceeds funded the difference and still built cash from $1,822m at FY2015-end to $19,628m at 3 May 2026.

Three features of the record matter for the forward view.

Buyback timing was good within the years the company acted and worse than mechanical across the decade. In six of the seven fiscal periods with repurchases the average price paid was below that year's average monthly close, and spreading each year's actual dollars evenly across its own months would have bought 799m shares against the 849m Broadcom bought. Spreading the same $43,593m evenly across the 102 months from November 2017 to April 2026 would have bought 912m shares at $47.78; Broadcom bought 849m at $51.35. The entire gap is FY2020 and FY2021, the only two years inside that window that drew zero repurchase dollars, while cash built from $5,055m to $12,163m waiting for an acquisition. Tan described the reasoning when the December 2021 authorization was announced: "we did not do a deal in '20, did not do a deal in '21. Got tons of cash... it's just a very logical conclusion for us to not just sit on the cash." That authorization was made in the month the stock set its FY2022 high, and the $7,000m spent under it was the only year in the record where the average price paid exceeded the fiscal year's average close.

The buyback has never reduced the share count. Split-adjusted diluted shares went from 3,830m in FY2016 to 4,853m in FY2025 and 4,876m in FQ2 FY2026, up 26.7%, despite $35,143m of open-market repurchase and $15,484m of tax-withholding repurchase. The step changes are acquisition consideration: +9.9% in FY2017 and +11.8% in FY2024, the latter being the 544m split-adjusted shares issued to VMware holders at a fair value of $53,398m, equal to 12.8% of the FY2023 diluted count. Across the seven years without an acquisition-driven step the count moved between −2.8% and +2.4%, so repurchases have offset annual issuance without shrinking the base.

The settlement mechanism changed in the second half of FY2025 and it flatters reported cash flow. Through FY2025 Broadcom net-settled vesting equity, withholding shares and paying the employee's tax in cash — $5,216m in FY2024 and $3,860m in FY2025. It now settles withholding "using proceeds from the sale of a portion of the vested shares", so the cash line was zero in the two quarters ended 3 May 2026 against $3,802m in the same half of FY2025. The change removes roughly $4-5bn a year of cash outflow, raises reported free cash flow by the same amount, and raises net equity-plan issuance from 33m to 42m shares half on half. FQ2 FY2026's record 46.3% free-cash-flow margin is not comparable to the FY2024 and FY2025 margins on the cash the company kept.

Per-share outcomes. Using FY2017 as the base, the first full year after the Broadcom Corporation merger:

Size growth reached the per-share line with about two points of annual leakage. Total shareholder return over the same eight years was 43.8% annualized. Against 19.9% annual free-cash-flow-per-share growth, the multiple on free cash flow per share went from 19.4x at the FY2017 close to 66.6x at the FY2025 close; the compounding is the capital allocation's work and the re-rating is not.

The dividend policy and the arithmetic behind it have separated. The stated policy since December 2016 is approximately 50% of prior-year free cash flow, last restated as policy on the FQ4 FY2022 call. Realized payout against prior-year free cash flow: 61.5% (FY2017), 53.3%, 51.4%, 56.5%, 51.0%, 50.5%, 46.9%, 55.7% (FY2024), 57.4% (FY2025) and roughly 46% on the FY2026 declaration. The FY2026 dividend was set at $0.65 a quarter, $2.60 for the year, a 10% increase and the fifteenth consecutive annual raise, announced in language that dropped the ratio: "Aligned with our ability to generate increased cash flows in the preceding year." FY2025 free cash flow grew 39%. The annual per-share increase has been 10-14% for six consecutive years regardless of what free cash flow did. On the FY2026 free-cash-flow run-rate the $2.60 declaration is roughly a quarter of the year it is earned in, so between $8bn and $9bn a year of dividend policy is unresolved from FY2027.

What the non-dividend half is for. Tan on the FQ4 FY2024 call: the two uses are parking cash for an acquisition or paying down debt, and "we're buying big enough companies, you almost say that 50% cash is sitting there is not adequate. So the likely use of that 50% cash is... pay down debt." On the same call, asked whether the acceleration of the business changed his appetite, he said "We are open, still open, always open." Leverage is the one hard constraint management names and it has been honoured: gross debt to adjusted EBITDA was under 2.5x by FY2025 year-end, two years after the VMware close, against the commitment made at announcement.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

Broadcom is a disciplined serial acquirer on the evidence available, and the two tests that usually expose a value-destroyer both come back clean. Across roughly $166,000m of announced consideration and thirteen fiscal years there has been no goodwill impairment, with the annual fourth-quarter test concluding no impairment in every year from FY2015 to FY2025.▪ Every large acquisition was followed by the sale of the parts management said at signing it did not want, each within three to thirteen months and at a gain or an immaterial loss, and none was forced by a regulator. In three cases the assets were classified held-for-sale inside the purchase-price allocation on day one.

11.2 What the announcement figures and the accounting figures mean

Three deals are quoted publicly at numbers that do not match the purchase-price tables, and both figures are correct on their own basis. Broadcom Corporation was announced at $37,000m against $35,706m recorded, because Avago's share price moved between announcement and closing on a fixed exchange ratio. Brocade was announced at $5,900m against $6,038m recorded, because the accounting total includes $701m paid to retire Brocade's term loan. VMware was announced at "approximately $61 billion" of equity against $86,290m recorded, because Broadcom's own shares rose from $53.16 to $98.12 split-adjusted between 25 May 2022 and 21 November 2023 on a fixed 2.52-share exchange ratio, so VMware holders captured that move; the $25,290m gap is Broadcom's own re-rating.

Against the multiple Broadcom itself traded at on the day before each announcement, every target except the Symantec assets came in below Broadcom's own revenue multiple: LSI at 2.8x against about 4.1x, Broadcom Corporation at 4.2x against about 5.8x, Brocade at 2.6x against about 5.8x, CA at 4.3x against about 5.7x, VMware at 6.6x against about 7.5x, and the Symantec assets at 6.3x against about 6.0x. Broadcom's answer on the one that did not is the cost line: the Symantec deck put the acquired business at 30.6x standalone EBITDA and 8.2x the $1,300m of pro forma EBITDA it said it would reach within twelve months.

The market's reaction to the CA announcement was the largest in the record. Broadcom's market capitalization went from $105,088m on 11 July 2018 to $90,644m on 12 July, a single-day decline of $14,444m, and the shares declined as much as 19% intraday to $197.46, an eighteen-month low (datacenterknowledge.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. That single-day loss is more than three quarters of the entire equity value of the target.

11.3 What the clean impairment record does and does not show

Goodwill is tested at two reporting units, $26,013m in semiconductors and $71,788m in infrastructure software. The Symantec deal put $6,638m of goodwill on the books, 9.2% of the software unit today, and CA $9,796m, 13.6%. A complete write-off of either would not by itself impair a unit whose fair value is now set mostly by VMware, so the absence of impairment is consistent with several individual deals having disappointed.

The purchase price runs through the income statement as amortization instead. Acquisition-related intangible amortization was $3,247m in FY2023, $9,267m in FY2024 and $8,062m in FY2025, with accumulated amortization of $18,917m at 2 November 2025. VMware's $40,842m of finite-lived intangibles amortize over eight to fourteen years, so roughly $5,000m a year of the purchase price runs through earnings regardless of how the business performs. Integration is not free either: restructuring and other charges totalled $5,213m across FY2016-FY2025, with the FY2024 spike of $1,787m being VMware employee terminations, plus $549m and $216m of acquisition-related costs in FY2024 and FY2025.

Segment margins are above the cash-on-cash return, because they exclude the two costs the deals created. In FY2025 the two segments summed to $41,997m of operating income against $25,484m reported, and the $16,513m difference is $8,062m of amortization, $7,568m of stock compensation, $667m of restructuring and $216m of acquisition costs.

11.4 What the acquired franchises did afterwards

The FY2019-to-FY2023 stretch is the CA and Symantec test with no VMware in it: segment revenue grew from $5,156m to $7,637m, a compound 10.3% that includes the first full year of Symantec, while the operating margin rose 8.0 points from 65.8% to 73.8%. Strip the Symantec step and the acquired revenue base was close to flat: CA and the Symantec assets arrived with roughly $6,000m of revenue between them, and the whole segment including Brocade was $7,385m in FY2022. Margin did the work.

VMware repeated that pattern faster. Management took VMware's quarterly spending from over $2,400m before the deal to $1,200m by FQ4 FY2024, and VMware contributed $12,384m of revenue to FY2024 continuing operations. Against the promise: the target was to lift VMware from about $4,700m of standalone EBITDA to about $8,500m of pro forma run-rate EBITDA within three years of closing, at "mid-60s%" EBITDA margins with the variance "going back into the sales and marketing investment". The segment produced $20,765m of operating income in FY2025 before stock compensation and amortization, which management said exceeded the $8,500m target early. The reinvestment did not happen: segment selling, general and administrative expense declined 27.2% in FY2025 and R&D declined 5.8%, and both declined again in each of the last two quarters.

11.5 Regulatory conditions and the programme's current state

The VMware clearance attached ten-year behavioural remedies to the Fibre Channel HBA franchise Broadcom bought with Emulex in 2015. The European Commission cleared the deal on 12 July 2023 conditional on giving Marvell — named as the only rival — interoperability APIs, materials, tools and technical support to develop and certify third-party Fibre Channel host bus adapters, an irrevocable open-source licence to the source code of all current and future Broadcom FC HBA drivers, and organisational separation between the HBA team and the certification team, monitored by an independent trustee (ec.europa.eu, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. The UK cleared it unconditionally in August 2023 and China's SAMR imposed its own conditions in November 2023 [web]. The deal took eighteen months from announcement to close; Brocade took twelve and a half.

The acquisition programme has stopped. Cash paid for acquisitions was $25,978m in FY2024, zero in FY2025 and zero in the first half of FY2026; goodwill has been $97,801m at every balance-sheet date since 2 November 2025. The last purchase of any size was the $600m of Seagate assets in April 2024, so Broadcom has been out of the market for more than two years, a longer gap than the twenty-four months between the Symantec close and the VMware announcement. The software franchise the programme built now compounds organically or not at all.

12. Capitalization and balance sheet

Every obligation is a senior unsecured fixed-rate instrument. There is no secured debt, no floating-rate debt, no convertible, no drawn revolver and no commercial paper outstanding; the last floating exposure, the $30,390m of 2023 Term Loans raised for VMware, was fully repaid during FY2025.

Notes issued from April 2019 are obligations of Broadcom Inc. guaranteed by Broadcom Technologies Inc. and Broadcom Corporation, which is why Moody's rates the guarantor's backed senior unsecured paper A2, one notch above Broadcom Inc. at A3.

Weighted-average cost of debt. Instrument by instrument, principal-weighted: a contractual cash coupon of 4.04% and a filed effective rate of 4.56% at 3 May 2026, on a weighted maturity of 7.5 years, for an annual cash coupon run-rate of about $2,698m.

The 52-basis-point gap between the two is concentrated in the assumed VMware notes, fair-valued at acquisition: $4,500m of principal at a 2.28% weighted coupon accrues at a 5.64% effective rate, so cash interest on that tranche is about $103m a year against roughly $254m of GAAP interest, with the difference accreting the carrying value toward par. The CFO stated 4% and 7.2 years for $67.1bn at FY2025 year-end, which the instrument-level model reproduces at 3.98% and 7.1 years.

Maturity wall and refinancing cost. Only $12,527m, 18.8% of the stack, matures through FY2029, at a 3.84% weighted coupon. The January 2026 issuance priced at 4.30% for five years, 4.60% for seven, 4.95% for ten and 5.70% for thirty, so refinancing the whole FY2026-FY2029 wall at that curve adds roughly $100m of annual coupon [estimate: bucket by bucket], immaterial against LTM EBITDA of $41,360m. The larger repricing is deferred: the debt was fair-valued at $62,505m against $66,720m of principal at 3 May 2026, so the market prices the stack at about 94% of par and refinancing the whole thing at the January 2026 curve would cost roughly 4.6-5.0% [estimate: the new-issue curve interpolated to the 7.5-year weighted maturity gives about 4.7%; the current-price approximation gives about 5.0%], adding roughly $400-650m a year. That bill arrives in the 2030s. The $21,500m issued in 2021 at a 3.15% weighted coupon is the expensive refinancing and it matures 2031-2051.

Leases and pension. Operating lease liabilities were $1,325m at FY2025 year-end on an eleven-year weighted remaining term, there are no finance leases, and the frozen US pension plan was underfunded by $39m against $1,197m of assets. None of the three is material to the capital structure. Other contractual commitments for IT and services were $4,105m at 3 May 2026.

The obligation that appeared in one quarter. Unconditional purchase commitments went from $132m at 2 November 2025 and $54m at 1 February 2026 to $128,110m at 3 May 2026, with $22m falling in the FY2026 remainder, $55,214m in FY2027, $72,870m in FY2028 and $4m in FY2029. The definition is unchanged across all three filings. The FQ2 FY2026 risk factors explain the mechanism: customers "may make and have made greater demands on us with regards to pricing and contractual terms, such as seeking to lease our custom AI accelerators or XPUs or requiring us to purchase and then lease to them full AI racks or systems." Buying full racks means buying memory, CPUs, power and mechanical content Broadcom does not design.

Total obligations. At 3 May 2026 Broadcom had $66,720m of debt principal, $1,325m of lease liabilities, $39m of pension underfunding, $128,110m of purchase commitments and $4,105m of other contractual commitments, plus a $29bn maximum-exposure backstop entered five weeks later. Against $19,628m of cash and $164.6bn of remaining performance obligations. Those items settle over different periods and against different counterparties, so their sum is not a leverage measure. On funded debt the ratios are conventional and improving: gross debt to LTM EBITDA of 1.61x and net debt to LTM EBITDA of 1.14x at 3 May 2026, against 1.97x and 1.43x at FY2025 year-end and peaks above 3x after each of the three debt-funded acquisitions. The FY2026 deleveraging is not repayment — gross debt went $67,120m to $67,970m to $66,720m across the last two quarters, a $400m reduction — it is EBITDA growing 21% above the FY2025 figure after two quarters.

What the funded-debt ratios do not describe is the $128,110m of purchases falling due across two fiscal years, which no published leverage ratio includes. The three agencies also disagree on the funded figure: S&P puts adjusted leverage at 1.2x for FY2025, Fitch at 1.6x, and Moody's expects below 1.5x by FY2026 from about 3x at FY2024; gross debt over filed-statement EBITDA is 1.97x at FY2025 year-end. The spread across published numbers for one balance sheet is 0.8 of a turn.

Liquidity. Cash of $19,628m at 3 May 2026, an undrawn $7,500m five-year revolver maturing January 2030, and an unused $4,000m commercial paper programme. Cash covers short-term debt 8.7x. Broadcom also sells trade receivables on a non-recourse basis, $7,401m in FY2025 and $2,350m in the two quarters ended 3 May 2026 against $3,951m in the year-ago half, so factoring volume of roughly $7bn a year is about 10% of revenue and is discretionary; it was cut sharply while receivables rose 52%.

Ratings. Moody's upgraded to A3 from Baa1 on 22 September 2025 with a positive outlook, and the guarantor's backed senior unsecured paper to A2 (investing.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. At the January 2026 notes S&P rated the issuer A- with a positive outlook and Fitch BBB+ (investing.com, accessed 2026-08-14) [web]. Broadcom's own filings disclose no ratings.

Stock compensation and the share count.

The FY2024 step is VMware; the FY2025 step is the Two-Year Equity Awards granted in FQ2 FY2025 in place of that year's annual grant, which added $2,846m of FY2025 expense on their own and vest over four to five years. Because that grant covered two years, FY2026 has no annual grant, and the schedule was fixed in advance: $8,301m in FY2026, $7,118m in FY2027, $4,985m in FY2028, $2,689m in FY2029 and $740m thereafter, $23,833m in total at 2 November 2025. First-half FY2026 expense of $4,268m already annualizes above the FY2026 line. The FY2027 grant decision falls inside the forecast period.

Fully neutralising equity-plan issuance would cost roughly $28-33bn a year [estimate: 42m shares issued in H1 FY2026 annualizes to 84m, at the $338 average H1 repurchase price or the $395.08 August close], against LTM free cash flow of $32,762m and a dividend run-rate of about $12.4bn. On the FQ3 FY2026 guided run-rate those two claims fit inside free cash flow; on the trailing-twelve-month base they do not.

Structural risks, ordered by the dollar exposure disclosed or estimable. The largest is the $128,110m of purchase commitments together with the $29bn backstop, $157bn of obligation created in one quarter and both outside published leverage ratios. Next is single-customer credit concentration inside that backstop, whose remedies on default leave Broadcom holding custom silicon built for that customer. Working capital is absorbing the ramp: receivables rose to $10,830m from $7,145m and inventory to $4,328m from $2,270m while factoring halved. Equity-plan dilution runs at $8,785m of LTM expense against a share count that has risen in each of the last two fiscal years and in the first half of FY2026 despite $8,450m of repurchases. Refinancing is modest and floating-rate and currency exposure is nil. Covenant proximity cannot be tested: no financial maintenance covenant is published in the 10-K, the 10-Qs or the 2025 credit agreement 8-K, and the revolver is undrawn.

Book equity of $87,691m at 3 May 2026 stands against $97,801m of goodwill and $28,333m of net intangibles, so tangible book value is negative $38,443m. There is no asset coverage behind the debt; the coverage is cash flow, at 13.2x interest on LTM EBITDA.

13.3 What actually drove the numbers

Gross margin rose from 44.9% in FY2016 to 67.8% in FY2025 for three reasons: the mix shift into infrastructure software, which ran at 93% gross margin in FY2025 and grew from nothing to 42% of revenue; the exit of low-margin semiconductor product lines; and the depletion between FY2019 and FY2021 of the Broadcom Corporation intangible base that had been charged to cost of revenue.

Operating margin is dominated by acquisition accounting. GAAP operating margin has moved between −3.1% and 45.2% inside the window because acquisition-intangible amortization moved between $2.6bn and $9.4bn a year and stock compensation between $0.7bn and $7.6bn. The FY2024-to-FY2025 recovery of 13.8 points decomposes cleanly: amortization plus restructuring declined from 21.4% of revenue to 13.7%, which is 7.8 of the points, and product cost plus the two operating-expense lines contributed the other 6.0.

Component FY2024, % of revenue FY2025, % of revenue Contribution
Product and service cost of revenue 24.8 22.7 +2.1 pts
Acquisition-intangible amortization in cost of revenue 11.7 9.4 +2.3 pts
Restructuring in cost of revenue 0.5 0.1 +0.4 pts
Gross margin 63.0 67.8 +4.8 pts

Operating margin 26.1 39.9 +13.8 pts

Returns on capital repeat a pattern twice. A large acquisition drops return on invested capital sharply, to the 6% area in FY2017 and FY2019-FY2020 and to 13.1% in FY2024; four to five years of amortization run-off and organic profit growth then lift it into the 24-28% area (FY2022-FY2023). The trailing twelve months to FQ2 FY2026 is 21.1% [estimate: TTM operating income of $32,746m times 0.85 over average invested capital of $131,610m], already above FY2025 and rising every quarter. On the specific question of whether VMware paid: infrastructure software segment operating income rose from $5,639m in FY2023 to $20,765m in FY2025, $15,126m of increase against $76,868m of incremental invested capital between the same two dates, which is 19.7% pre-tax and 16.7% after the ten-year cash tax rate. That figure excludes the stock compensation and amortization the deal created; deducting both gives 11.0-11.8% on the full acquisition cost.

Free cash flow conversion. Cumulatively Broadcom converted $79,230m of net income into $130,872m of free cash flow over the decade, a ratio of 1.65x, because $52,974m of acquired-intangible amortization never touched cash. Conversion against EBITDA has declined from 1.06x in FY2020 to 0.79x in FY2025 as cash interest and cash taxes rose: cash interest paid was $2,672m in FY2025 against $1,503m in FY2023, and cash taxes $2,589m against $1,782m. Cumulative capital expenditure over ten years was $5,812m, 1.9% of cumulative revenue and 1.11x depreciation excluding acquisition amortization, so the physical asset base is being maintained and not expanded.

Cash taxes. Broadcom paid $11,554m of cash tax on $76,873m of cumulative pre-tax income across ten years, a 15.0% rate, and reported a net GAAP tax benefit in four of the ten years including $8,084m in FY2018 and $397m in FY2025. Tax incentives and holidays reduced the FY2025 provision by $2,709m and added $0.56 to diluted EPS. Management guided a non-GAAP rate of approximately 16% for FY2026 on the global minimum tax and geographic mix, and the FQ2 FY2026 10-Q states the company expects to remain subject to the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax while maintaining a full valuation allowance against its CAMT credit carryforwards. The historical 15% is not a forward rate.

Restatements and basis changes inside the window. Segments went from four to three in FY2019 and three to two in FY2020, with no comparable revenue series spanning the first change. The SG&A allocation was refined in FQ4 FY2020, moving FY2019 semiconductor segment operating income from $8,150m to $8,538m. FY2017 operating income was restated from $2,383m to $2,371m. The 10-for-1 split took effect 15 July 2024. And in FY2025 $7,800m of upfront licence revenue was included in products revenue, with $4,601m for FY2024 and $1,058m for FY2023 reclassified from subscriptions and services to conform, so the products-against-subscriptions split is not comparable to earlier filings; total revenue is unaffected.

They part company on what follows: consensus takes revenue to $345,140m by FY2030, a five-year compound rate of 40.1% from the FY2025 base, and in 865 company-years starting above $50bn of revenue the best five-year outcome observed is 29.3%.▪

Consolidated revenue, FY2028 Not guided; FY2028 described as "substantial growth" over FY2027 $229,361m, +53.1% a year from FY2025, on 37 contributing estimates Management gives no number, so this is the street alone Zero of 1,009 company-years starting above $50bn compounded at +53.1% over three years; the class maximum is +42.0%
Consolidated revenue, FY2030 Not guided $345,140m, +40.1% a year, on five contributing estimates Five estimates is not a market view Zero of 865 company-years cleared +40.1% over five years; the maximum is +29.3%, which applied to Broadcom gives $232bn against consensus $345bn
Gross margin ~74% for FQ3 FY2026, down 310 basis points; investors asked to model the two segments separately 75.1% FY2026, 73.0% FY2027, 72.4% FY2028, non-GAAP No disagreement on direction. Mizuho expects long-term margin in the low-to-mid 70s against a prior expectation above 77% Gross margin above 65% at revenue above $20bn: median −2.6 points over five years, 29% expanded
Operating margin ~67% for FQ3 FY2026, flat sequentially, on flat operating expense 66.6%, 65.3%, 66.1% non-GAAP through FY2028, then 63.6% by FY2030 Consensus holds operating margin while gross margin declines 6.0 points, which needs operating expense to fall from 13.1% of revenue in FY2025 to 6.4% in FY2028 GAAP operating margin above 35% at revenue above $10bn: median −5.0 points over five years, 29.2% expanded. Broadcom's trailing four quarters at 43.4% is the 99.0th percentile at its scale
Free cash flow ~40% of revenue as the standing bar; 46% delivered in FQ2 FY2026 47.8% FY2026, 51.9% FY2027, 52.0% FY2028 Consensus embeds no working-capital absorption, in a period when days of inventory rose 28 in two quarters and factoring halved Free-cash-flow margin above 35% at revenue above $20bn: median −12.2 points over five years. Consensus FY2027 conversion is above every non-financial observation in 1,034 company-years above $50bn
Capital expenditure ~2% of revenue as the standing ceiling; 1.0% delivered 1.0%, 0.8%, 0.8% of revenue Consensus is below the current run-rate of 1.16% for the half, in the year the 10-K says capex will be higher Not a constraint at this level
Dividend and share count ~50% of prior-year free cash flow; $2.60 declared for FY2026; about 4.94bn diluted shares guided for FQ3 DPS $2.88, $3.31, $4.47 for FY2026-FY2028 Consensus dividend per share grows 15-35% a year while the declared per-share increase has been 10-14% for six years The count has risen in each of the last two fiscal years and in the first half of FY2026

Consensus has followed management and not led it: FY2027 revenue has doubled and FY2027 adjusted EPS has risen 93.1% over twelve months, tracking the sequence of upward revisions Broadcom issued on its own calls, and every revision in that period has been upward on revenue and EPS and downward on gross margin.▪ The distribution is entirely on one side: 56 buy-equivalent ratings, five hold-equivalent and no sell ratings on 61 rated analysts, with the lowest published twelve-month target of $400 inside the $395.00-$417.82 range the shares traded in around this date, so no contributor models Broadcom below what management has already told them. And coverage thins sharply past FY2028 — 52 estimates for FY2027, 32 for FY2028, six for FY2029 and four for FY2030 — so the last two consensus years are a thin extrapolation.

Across the ten available Broadcom sell-side reports, none discusses the distributor at 42% of net revenue, none discusses termination rights, contract liabilities or remaining performance obligations against the $128.7bn gap between cited backlog and filed RPO, and none discusses operating expense or research and development against a consensus path that takes operating expense from 13.1% of revenue to 6.4%.

The perfect-foresight column divides each fiscal-year-end price by the next year's actual non-GAAP EPS, so it uses hindsight the market did not have; the FY2025 entry of 32x is the exception, using the FY2026 consensus of $11.57. The GAAP trailing series is dominated by acquisition accounting, swinging between 7.8x in FY2018, when a one-time tax benefit lifted GAAP net income to $12,259m, and 137x in FY2024, when VMware amortization and a $4,238m tax charge cut it to $5,895m; the non-GAAP series is the one the market has used. EV/EBITDA uses Bloomberg's GAAP-basis EBITDA of $34,441m for FY2025; on management's adjusted EBITDA of $43,000m the FY2025 figure is 42x instead of 52x, and the gap is stock compensation. Price-to-book declined from 14.5x at FY2023-end to 11.7x at FY2024-end while the shares doubled, because VMware purchase accounting nearly tripled common equity from $23,988m to $67,678m. Book value has not been how this company is priced; the ten-year P/B median is 9.4x with a minimum of 2.8x and a maximum of 26.1x.

From the FY2016 close to the FY2025 close the share price multiplied 21.8x: forward consensus EPS multiplied 7.0x, from $1.35 to $9.38, and the forward multiple 3.1x, from 12.6x to 39.4x, so multiple expansion accounted for 37% of the log return and estimate growth for 63%. Dividends contributed 602 points over the same span, with a price return of +2,083% against a total return of +2,684%.

Fiscal 2026 to date inverts that. Forward consensus EPS is up 88.1% since the FY2025 close, the largest single-year estimate increase in the eleven-year record, while the forward multiple contracted 39.9% from 39.4x to 23.7x, the largest contraction in the record, against FY2022's −31.8% and FY2018's −28.8%. The shares are up 13.0% fiscal-year-to-date.

Revenue beat in 11 of 12 and non-GAAP EPS in 12 of 12, and only 6 of 12 next-session reactions were positive. Quarter Reaction What the market reacted to
FQ3 FY2023 −5.5% Tan on the call: "without the benefit of generative AI revenue in Q3, our semiconductor business was approximately flat year-on-year." The print was in line and the VMware deal was still awaiting approval
FQ1 FY2024 −7.0% AI revenue quadrupled to $2.3bn, and management held the FY2024 consolidated guide at approximately $50bn set the prior December. The AI number rose; the total did not
FQ2 FY2024 +12.3% The largest revenue beat of the twelve at +3.5%, a raised FY2024 AI outlook, a statement that non-AI had bottomed, and the announcement of the 10-for-1 split
FQ3 FY2024 −10.4% Revenue beat 0.4% but the FQ4 guide of approximately $14.0bn landed below the consensus the market held. The quarter also posted a GAAP net loss of $1,875m on a $4,238m tax charge
FQ4 FY2024 +24.4% The only revenue miss in the twelve produced the best day in the company's history: FY2024 AI revenue of $12.2bn, up 220%, and a $60-90bn FY2027 serviceable market across three hyperscale customers with million-accelerator cluster roadmaps. Market capitalization passed $1trn
FQ1 FY2025 +8.6% AI revenue of $4.1bn beat management's own $3.8bn forecast, the FQ2 AI guide went to $4.4bn, and the customer pipeline widened beyond the original three
FQ2 FY2025 −5.0% The CFO guided FQ3 consolidated gross margin "down approximately 130 basis points sequentially, primarily reflecting a higher mix of XPUs within AI revenue"
FQ3 FY2025 +9.4% A fourth accelerator customer qualified with over $10bn of rack orders, disclosed on the call and not in the release; consolidated backlog of $110bn
FQ4 FY2025 −11.4% The second-largest revenue beat of the twelve produced the second-worst reaction. Management disclosed $162bn of consolidated backlog including $73bn of AI orders over eighteen months, and the AI figure was judged light against the shipment ramp
FQ2 FY2026 −12.6% Revenue and AI revenue both beat and FQ3 was guided to $29.4bn, +84%. Against that, gross margin was guided down to approximately 74% from 77.1%, Tan conceded source diversity at Google, and the FY2027 AI figure was reiterated at "in excess of $100 billion" and not raised

Broadcom's FY2026 consensus EPS has been revised up 40.0% over twelve months and its FY2027 consensus up 93.1%. Across the 35 companies in the table that places Broadcom eighth on the FY2026 revision and fifth on the FY2027 revision, behind Credo (+192.9%), Astera Labs (+122.1%), ASE Technology (+114.1%) and AMD (+98.2%), the first two of which have market capitalizations of $50bn and $56bn. Among the seven companies above $1trn of market capitalization, Broadcom's FY2027 revision is the largest: TSMC +65.3%, NVIDIA +49.3%, Alphabet +28.1%, Apple +9.3%, Microsoft +8.3%, Meta −4.8%.

17. Forward model summary

Broadcom's share of Google's TPU volume is not established, and Google is the largest component of the unit driver that ranks first in the sensitivity table. Every scenario treats that share through the unit assumption and none tests it directly.

17.1 The driver tree

Revenue is built from four terms and not from a company growth rate.

Consolidated revenue ├── Semiconductor Solutions │ ├── AI semiconductor │ │ ├── XPU revenue = XPU units × XPU ASP │ │ └── AI networking = XPU revenue × [share ÷ (1 − share)] │ └── Non-AI semiconductor = prior year × (1 + growth) └── Infrastructure Software = prior year × (1 + growth)

The identity reproduces FY2025 to within $21m of the four disclosed quarters (2.3m units at $5,700 divided by 0.65 gives $20,169m against $20,190m) and FY2026 to within 1% of the guide (2.6m at $13,500 divided by 0.62 gives $56,613m against approximately $56,000m).▪

Units and price are used instead of gigawatts because the gigawatt driver is ambiguous by a factor of two. Management guides roughly 10 GW for FY2027 and AI revenue "in excess of $100 billion", about $10bn per gigawatt, against a stated content figure of $15-20bn. Two analysts asked for the reconciliation and neither received one. The likely difference is scope, with the higher figure a system-sale number and the guide chip-only, and no filing says so. Year 0 is FY2025 and every FY2025 line is copied from the audited figures without adjustment.

Cumulative free cash flow FY2026-FY2032 is $702,235m and cumulative working-capital absorption is $27,580m.

The base departs from management nowhere through FY2027: the FY2026 AI line is the $56bn guide plus the 1% median beat of the last seven AI guides, the FY2027 AI line of $109,701m falls between the ">$100 billion" floor and the roughly $112bn implied by Tan's "in the range of 2x", and FY2026 software holds the "low double-digit" framework.▪ The departures begin in FY2028, where management has said only "substantial growth".

One line needs a caveat. First-half FY2026 free cash flow was $18,272m, 44.0% of half-year revenue, so the FY2026 figure of $51,200m requires $32,928m in the second half on $62,915m of revenue, a 52.3% margin against a record 46.3% in FQ2. The mechanism is operating leverage on a revenue base that roughly doubles half on half while acquisition-intangible amortization stays near $2,000m a quarter and the cost base is fabless. That margin is the least supported assumption in FY2026.

Revenue compound rates from FY2025: bear +14.4% a year to FY2030 and +12.5% to FY2032; base +27.8% and +22.3%; bull +42.7% and +32.1%. Cumulative AI semiconductor revenue over FY2026-FY2030 is $377,892m in the bear, $649,174m in the base and $1,061,373m in the bull, the last of which matches JPMorgan's estimate of over $1trn of cumulative AI revenue through 2030.

The bear is below every published estimate: the lowest Bloomberg contributor for FY2027 revenue is $157,819m and the lowest published price target is $400 against the $417.82 close, so the downside case has to be constructed from the drivers.

The bull asks for incremental economics slightly better than the segment has ever delivered: consolidated incremental operating margins of 68%, 69%, 70%, 68% and 68% in FY2026, FY2027, FY2028, FY2029 and FY2031, against a realized semiconductor segment incremental operating margin of 67% over FY2018-FY2025 and 66-68% in the AI-era quarters. The consolidated FY2025 figure of 97.6% is not a counter-example, because it came from amortization and restructuring falling from 21.4% of revenue to 13.7%. No bear or base year exceeds the 67% rate.

Base FY2032 operating income is $141,969m and base cumulative free cash flow is $702,235m, so the unit swing alone is 35% of terminal operating income and 27% of the cumulative cash. Networking share ranks above accelerator gross margin because it moves revenue and margin together: each point of share added is revenue at a 75% gross margin displacing nothing. Software growth ranks fourth on terminal operating income because it compounds, and at 93% gross margin almost all of a revenue difference reaches operating income. Working capital does not touch operating income and moves cumulative free cash flow by 3.0%; the level assumption matters less than the $27,580m of absorption already inside the base.
