The FY2029 and FY2030 consensus lines come from six and five contributing revenue estimates against 55 for FY2027.

Against the outside view, the base case is not a conservative case. Its five-year revenue compound rate of +27.8% from the FY2025 base implies FY2030 revenue of $217,573m, which places it between the 99th percentile ($182bn) and the observed maximum ($232bn, Amazon FY2015-FY2020) of 865 company-years starting above $50bn of revenue. On the better-covered three-year test the base at +47.0% a year exceeds the class maximum of +42.0% in 1,009 company-years. The bear at +14.4% over five years is between the 90th and 95th percentiles. Consensus at +40.1% and the bull at +42.7% are above every observation in the class. Two things the class cannot see place the base there: $164,600m of remaining performance obligations at 3 May 2026 against $33,300m six months earlier, and a management record of setting a number and beating it across seven consecutive quarters of AI guidance, one full-year AI guide beaten by 22%, and a VMware EBITDA target cleared roughly a year early.

17.7 Assumptions and where each is contested

Eight of the twenty-seven drivers are supported by the evidence at their base value: FY2026 AI revenue, non-AI gross margin, software gross margin, acquisition-intangible amortization, restructuring, the tax rate, interest expense and depreciation. The rest are contested, and the direction is not uniform. The evidence points above the base on FY2027 accelerator units, on the networking share of AI revenue, on software growth in the terminal years, on capital expenditure and on stock-based compensation; it points below the base on accelerator gross margin, on the depth of the digestion year, on the FY2026 software line and on working capital; and it points against the base in both directions on the dividend payout and the share count, which cannot both hold alongside the model's own cash generation. The networking share is the one driver where every disclosed observation lies above both the base and the bear.

Assumption Bear / base / bull Basis Where it is contested
AI semiconductor revenue, FY2026 54,702 / 56,613 / 60,097 ($m) Management guidance of approximately $56,000m, 3 June 2026, plus the median beat of the last seven AI guides Three of four quarters are reported or guided; 25 of 25 consolidated revenue guides and 7 of 7 AI guides have been met or beaten, with the beat narrowing to +0.9% as the guide became a shipment schedule
XPU units shipped, FY2027 3.6 / 4.2 / 4.9 (m) Management's roughly 10 GW plan and the disclosed accelerator share of AI revenue Three angles put FY2027 units above the base: Morgan Stanley reports Broadcom booking 365k of 2027 CoWoS-S wafers, of which about 330k implies roughly 3.9m units for Google alone, leaving little for five other customers; $55,214m of FY2027 purchase commitments exceeds modelled FY2027 semiconductor cost of revenue by $10,346m; and the base implies about $11bn of AI revenue per gigawatt against management's cited $15-20bn. The band should widen upward to roughly 3.6-5.5m with the base nearer 4.5m
XPU units shipped, FY2032 4.0 / 6.4 / 10.3 (m) Terminal level after the build wave The base path contains one 10% unit decline and a terminal level 3% above the FY2029 peak. The 37-company technology drawdown class lost a median 37.9% of revenue peak to trough, 12 of 37 never regained the peak, and among those that did the median took seven years. The base should sit lower or the bear should extend well below 4.0m
XPU ASP, FY2027 16,500 / 17,500 / 19,500 ($) The FY2026 price of about $13,500 plus one generational content step The bear is mislabelled: $16,500 against $13,500 is +22% and not flat content. The largest input to the base step is deflating, with HBM3E contract prices $13-17/GB against a $17-20 peak. Units and price are also not independently observable — only their product is constrained — so the ±20% unit and ±15% price rows in the sensitivity table partly double-count the same uncertainty
XPU ASP, FY2032 17,000 / 21,800 / 23,500 ($) Content per unit stepping with each generation A ±15% band six years out on a quantity that moved 2.35x in one year, with the bull only 7.8% above the base. The band should run at least $14,000 to $28,000
AI networking share of AI revenue, FY2029 28% / 30% / 36% Management's stated steady state of about 30% Every disclosed observation exceeds both the base and the bear: 40%, 40%, 35%, 33% and almost 40% across five quarters, mean about 38%, minimum 33%. This is the one forward figure where management has a 0-for-3 record, missing in the same direction each time. Networking content per accelerator roughly doubled between FY2025 and FY2026, Tomahawk 6 is sold out, and Tomahawk 7 taped out in FQ2 FY2026. The evidence supports a base of 33-35% with a range of 30-40%. At ±5 points this driver is worth $21,465m of FY2032 operating income
AI revenue change in the digestion year −22% / −7% / 0% Semiconductor cohort downside base rates One −7% year in seven, against a cohort that declined in 28.8% of company-years since FY2010 with 11.0% down more than 10%. A −7% single year is at the shallow end of observed declines and the shape is too benign; the class supports either a deeper drawdown or a second down year inside the seven. The bull's assertion of no down year at all is what consensus does and what the class contradicts most directly
Non-AI semiconductor growth 0% / +3% / +6% a year Below the semiconductor class median of +8.2% and above the realized three-year trend The bear excludes the modal recent outcome: the line declined 26.6% in FY2024 and 6.9% in FY2025 and is 28% below FY2023. The base survives on FQ2 FY2026 bookings above $6,000m against $4,200m shipped and a +12% FQ3 guide. Materiality is low, at $4,825m of FY2032 operating income across the swing
XPU gross margin, FY2028 onward 52% / 58% / 64% Two-equation solves at 64-68% and a bill-of-materials stack at 57-66%, plus what the FQ3 FY2026 guide already requires The company's own commitment schedule points lower: $55,214m of FY2027 purchases against modelled FY2027 semiconductor revenue of $127,829m implies a segment gross margin of at most 56.8% if consumed in year, against the modelled 64.9%. FY2028 repeats it at $72,870m against $61,112m of modelled cost. The band should extend below 52% until the composition of the $128,110m is known
AI networking gross margin 72% / 75% / 78% Residual solve at 75-80% This is a residual of a residual: filed segment cost of revenue, into a two-equation solve, into an assumed 40% networking share, into 75-80%. Moving the assumed share from 40% to 35% moves the implied margin by several points, and the share assumption is the one every disclosed observation contradicts. The band should run roughly 70% to 80%
Non-AI semiconductor gross margin 63% / 65.5% / 67% Two well-conditioned solves at 65.3% and 66.4% The observable series has declined roughly 4 points in two years from an implied 70% in FY2023, but the FY2023 mix is not the current mix and the two solves bracket the base within 1.1 points. Non-AI is 8% of FY2032 base revenue, so a 2-point error is about $420m
Semiconductor segment operating expense, FY2029 8,500 / 7,800 / 7,300 ($m) Segment R&D and SG&A growing about 20% a year through FY2028, faster than the realized 9.3% and slower than revenue The base takes segment operating expense to 4.1% of segment revenue from 10.5% in FY2025, the same fall in research intensity that makes the consensus operating-margin path hard to hold. The roadmap load does not fall over that window: six accelerator accounts across multiple generations, working 400G SerDes for the next TPU, Tomahawk 7, co-packaged optics and PCIe. Holding the FQ2 FY2026 intensity of 7.7% would give $14.8bn in FY2029, roughly twice the base. A ±9% band on a line that could plausibly be twice the base is not a scenario range
Infrastructure software revenue, FY2026 29,400 / 30,200 / 30,800 ($m) First-half actual plus the FQ3 guide, with FQ4 inside management's "low double-digit" framework The bear does not cover the risk in the FQ3 term: the $8,900m guide requires roughly $3.5-3.9bn of upfront licence revenue in one quarter, about 1.9x the year-ago quarter and roughly the whole of the first half. Upfront recognition depends on customers signing away termination rights at signature and not on demand. If that cohort slips out of FY2026 the year is roughly $26.5bn, 12% below the base. Software also produced the only segment-level guidance shortfall since quarterly segment guidance began, FQ4 FY2024 at 3.3% below on deals slipping
Infrastructure software growth, FY2027 +3% / +7% / +11% Non-upfront growth of 6.5-8.8% in the two FY2026 quarters, blended against legacy decay The component arithmetic does not reach 7%: VMware grew 13% on roughly 71% of the base while legacy declined 18-23% on the rest, blending to +3.4%, and letting VMware's share rise to 75% still gives only +4.8%. Reaching +7% needs the ARR-to-revenue convergence or the renewal cohort. The components support +4% to +5%
Infrastructure software growth, FY2030-FY2032 +2% / +4% / +7% a year Below the software class median because the repricing is complete The entire band is below the reference class: software at a $20bn revenue base has a median five-year forward CAGR of +8.4%, p75 +11.8% and p90 +14.3%, so the bull is below the class median. The legacy drag also falls from about 5.5 points of the blend in FY2026 to about 1.5 points by FY2032 as the declining base shrinks. The base should move toward 5-6%
Infrastructure software gross margin 91.5% / 93.0% / 93.0% Segment cost of revenue at 7.0% of revenue; management stated 93% on both FY2026 calls The segment is roughly 95% software blended with 60-68% hardware at 6-8% of segment revenue, so the only route above 93% is shrinking a small bounded line. The bull equalling the base is a real limitation and it is worth about $100m of FY2029 operating income
Infrastructure software operating expense growth +15% / +9% / +10% a year Cost removal has a floor: the segment spends less on R&D than VMware alone did standalone The scenario set is inverted — the bull spends more than the base, so the upside case is penalized on this row. The base also reverses an observed trend with no observed inflection: segment R&D declined 9.8% and 11.2% year on year in the two FY2026 quarters and SG&A declined 27.2% in FY2025
Stock-based compensation growth, FY2027-FY2029 +18% / +15% / +10% a year The filed schedule covers only existing grants, and the FY2027 grant decision falls inside the forecast The base takes stock compensation from 11.8% of revenue in FY2025 to 6.3% in FY2032, reversing the direction of a decade in which it grew 11.1x while revenue grew 4.8x. It also embeds $2,772m, $6,389m and $10,391m of undisclosed new-grant expense in FY2027-FY2029, and the dollars depend on a grant-date share price the model does not forecast. Consensus is further out on the same line, holding the total add-back near $11,000m a year while revenue doubles
Acquisition-intangible amortization, FY2027 6,805 with no scenario variance ($m) The filed expected-amortization schedule in the FY2025 10-K For FY2027 specifically, a deal closing in FY2026 or early FY2027 would add little FY2027 amortization. Zero variance across the whole seven years is a real limitation for a company that has bought a large software asset roughly every two years for a decade
Restructuring and acquisition costs, FY2028 700 / 400 / 300 ($m) FY2025 ran $883m and the VMware programme is winding down The full spread is 0.36% of FY2028 base operating income
Capital expenditure 1.5% / 1.2% / 1.0% of revenue FY2025 ran 1.0% and H1 FY2026 ran 1.16% with the Singapore packaging facility building The band excludes management's own stated ceiling of roughly 2%, and the realized ratio reached 3.05-6.06% in FY2016-FY2018. The FY2025 10-K states FY2026 capex will be higher. Materiality is small: 0.8 points of FY2032 revenue is $2.1bn against $128,886m of free cash flow
Net working capital 16% / 12% / 8% of revenue The realized level went from −10.8% of revenue at FY2024 year-end to +5.9% at FY2025 year-end to about +10.1% at 3 May 2026 The level has moved 21 points in eighteen months and is still moving, with every component pointing the same way, and the FY2027 commitment schedule implies roughly $10bn of goods bought and not consumed that the model does not hold as inventory. The bear at 16% should be the base and the bear should extend toward 20%
GAAP effective tax rate, FY2029 onward 20% / 17% / 15% Management's guided ~16% non-GAAP rate for FY2026 against a ten-year cash rate of 15.0% The base is above every historical observation, and the amortization shield that produced them runs off inside the forecast while the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax and the global minimum tax both set a 15% floor against book income
Interest expense, FY2028 3,100 / 2,850 / 2,700 ($m) $66,720m at a 4.04% cash coupon, entirely fixed-rate, with only $12,527m maturing through FY2029 The base is slightly below the clean run-rate of about $3,000m, and the full spread is 0.36% of FY2028 base operating income
Depreciation, FY2029 1,300 / 1,250 / 1,500 ($m) $574m in FY2025 on $2,530m of net property, scaling with the capex path Broadcom's property implies an average life above eight years, so the buildings-and-tooling spend does not depreciate on a five-year schedule. Depreciation is non-cash and adds back, so the range moves free cash flow by nothing
Diluted share count, FY2032 5,440 / 5,151 / 4,500 (m) The count rose in FY2024, FY2025 and H1 FY2026 despite $8,450m of repurchases Internally inconsistent with the model's own cash generation: cumulative free cash flow of $702,235m less $306,595m of dividends leaves roughly $396bn against $12,527m of debt maturing through FY2029, and the base then grows the count 0.8% a year, so roughly $400bn accumulates as cash. Broadcom has never done that. Either the surplus retires stock, taking the count toward the bull, or it buys a company, which breaks the zero-variance amortization assumption
Dividend payout 50% of prior-year free cash flow, no scenario variance The standing policy, last stated as such on the FQ4 FY2022 call Realized payout was 55.7% in FY2024 and 57.4% in FY2025, above the policy. Applying the ratio mechanically also produces per-share growth the company has never delivered: FY2032 dividends of $62,447m on 5,151m shares is $12.12 a share, 4.7x the FY2026 declaration and +29.3% a year, against a declared per-share increase of 10-14% for six consecutive years. Growing the declared figure at 10% instead gives about $4.60 a share and roughly $23.7bn, a $38.7bn difference in that year. The range should be 30% to 60%

17.8 What the model does not capture

The $29,000m maximum-exposure backstop entered on 8 June 2026 enters no line, because no liability is recognised and no schedule is published. Revenue recognition timing on sales into the Apollo and Blackstone vehicle is unmodelled, and whether Broadcom books on delivery to the vehicle or on deployment to the end customer changes the FY2027-FY2028 phasing. Acquisitions are assumed not to happen, so segment revenue is organic throughout and the amortization schedule runs off untouched. A single-counterparty credit event at the 42%-of-revenue distributor would move receivables and revenue together and is not modelled. The non-AI line moves as one number instead of five end markets. And whether the roughly 10 GW planned for 2027 is a fiscal or a calendar figure moves about two months of the steepest ramp between years.

One downside shape is missing and it is the one management's own mechanism implies. Every scenario above models share loss or a cycle break. Management says customers book eighteen to twenty-four months ahead because power paces them, so the live downside is a deferral: $55,214m of FY2027 purchase commitments arriving against revenue that slips two quarters, absorbed into inventory already at 86 days, with remaining performance obligations unchanged. That is a very different profit-and-loss and balance-sheet outcome from the scenarios shown.

18. Risks

Ranked by the dollar exposure disclosed or estimable in the filings, multiplied by the probability that the trigger occurs within the next eight quarters.

1. The $128.1bn of unconditional purchase commitments. Mechanism: Broadcom's manufacturing model was purchase-order based, and Item 1A still states "We do not generally have long-term capacity commitments with our CMs and substantially all of our manufacturing services are on a purchase order basis with no minimum quantities." The FQ2 FY2026 commitments table breaks that description, at $55,214m due in FY2027 and $72,870m in FY2028, defined as enforceable and legally binding with fixed or minimum quantities and price provisions, excluding anything cancellable without penalty. Exposure: 1.5x total stockholders' equity, 6.2x FY2025 total cost of revenue, and about 3.1x the annualized FQ2 FY2026 free cash flow run-rate. A customer order deferral does not reduce it. Leading indicators: the FY2027 and FY2028 rows of the commitments table each quarter; days of inventory (58, 68, 86 across three quarters); finished goods inside inventory ($682m to $1,858m); and the appearance of an inventory write-down. The disclosed offset is $164.6bn of remaining performance obligations entered in the same quarter, but 30% of that converts within twelve months while 100% of the purchases fall due by FY2029, and the customer contract's cancellation and repricing terms are not described.

2. The $29bn backstop on one customer's lease obligations. Exposure equals 33% of stockholders' equity and roughly 70% of the annualized FQ2 FY2026 free cash flow run-rate. Recovery on default depends on the resale value of deployed custom accelerators built to one customer's architecture, and the filing discloses no residual-value assumption and no accrued liability. The same customer is one of the six AI accounts, so a default and an order cancellation would be one event. Leading indicators: the maximum-exposure figure in each subsequent quarter; whether the backstop moves from a footnote to a recognized guarantee liability; the lessee's own funding announcements; and rating-agency commentary.

3. Gross-margin compression from AI mix. Consolidated gross margin was 77.1% in FQ2 FY2026 and is guided to approximately 74% on $29.4bn of revenue, a 310-basis-point step worth about $0.9bn of gross profit in one quarter, of which segment mix explains about a sixth. Networking was almost 40% of AI revenue against a stated normal level near 30%, so FQ2 was the high-water mark for segment margin and not the base. Leading indicators: AI networking as a percentage of AI revenue, disclosed only on the call; consolidated gross margin against the 74% guide on 2 September 2026; and whether gross-margin guidance continues to be given at all.

4. Customer concentration and second-sourcing at the largest programme. Sized in Section 4.7 at roughly $33-42bn of 2028 revenue for a 30-point share loss at Google [estimate: two sell-side model assumptions multiplied]. Leading indicators: the distributor and top-five percentages in each 10-Q; gigawatt commitments per customer against gigawatts shipped, on calls only; Alphabet's own capital-spending and TPU disclosures; and whether Broadcom continues to name six customers. A related and unresolved question runs the other way: if Broadcom retains the networking content on racks whose accelerator it loses, the exposure is much smaller and the margin effect runs the opposite direction, because networking is the richer half.

5. Customer-owned tooling and in-house displacement. Every one of the six AI customers is described by management as moving toward self-sufficiency: "each of them journeys at their own pace towards compute self-sufficiency" (FQ3 FY2025 call). The term entered Item 1A in the FQ1 FY2026 10-Q. The realized precedent inside Broadcom's own book is Apple, named at approximately 20% of net revenue in the FY2022 and FY2023 10-Ks and absent from FY2024 and FY2025. The precedent outside it is Alchip, which kept its design relationship and lost 39% of revenue in a year. Leading indicator: AI networking revenue holding while accelerator revenue at one customer slows, which is the pattern if a customer in-sources the accelerator and keeps buying switches.

6. Backlog cited on calls against remaining performance obligations filed. $162bn of consolidated backlog at FY2025 year-end against $33.3bn of filed RPO on the same date, a $128.7bn difference. The reconciling item is the termination-for-convenience exclusion, which covered 67% of FY2025 contract liabilities and 64% at 3 May 2026, and Broadcom does not draw it. This is a disclosure risk and not only a definitional one: the FY2025 10-K's legal proceedings describe a securities class action alleging that VMware's statements about backlog and related internal controls from August 2018 to February 2020 were materially misleading, where the court denied the motion to dismiss in April 2023 and a settlement was approved in March 2025.

7. Software revenue quality and the FQ3 FY2026 step. Upfront licence revenue supplied 58% of FY2025 segment growth. Software grew 1% year on year in FQ1 FY2026 and 9% in FQ2, and FQ3 is guided to approximately $8.9bn, up 31% and up about $1.7bn sequentially. Total contract value booked declined from $10.4bn in FQ4 FY2025 to $9.2bn in FQ1 FY2026 and was not disclosed for FQ2; ARR growth slowed from 19% to 17%. Goodwill of $97,801m and intangibles of $28,333m total $126,134m against $87,691m of equity, and VMware goodwill was fixed at $54,206m in FQ2 FY2024 and has not been tested to impairment since. A software renewal shortfall is the trigger that would test it.

8. Tax. Tax incentives and holidays reduced the FY2025 provision by $2,709m and added $0.56 to diluted EPS. The FY2025 10-K expected the global minimum tax to materially increase the effective rate for FY2026; the FQ1 FY2026 10-Q upgraded that to "have materially increased". A $1,058m valuation allowance was established against CAMT credit carryforwards in FQ3 FY2025 and a full allowance is maintained. The non-GAAP rate is guided to approximately 16% against realized quarterly effective rates near zero to 5% through the first half of FY2025.

9. Single foundry, single fabs, memory allocation. Approximately 95% of contract-manufactured wafers came from TSMC in FY2025 and in the first half of FY2026, unchanged across all eight 10-Qs examined. More than three-quarters of manufacturing materials come from five suppliers, some single-source; Fort Collins is the sole source for FBAR filters and Breinigsville for InP wafers. The $128,110m of purchase commitments is the price Broadcom paid to convert this into a fixed obligation, which links this risk to the first. Leading indicators: the 95% figure; the materials-concentration sentence; memory pricing.

10. Balance sheet and dilution. Debt of $66,720m against goodwill plus intangibles of $126,134m and equity of $87,691m, so tangible book value is negative $38,443m; coverage is cash flow at 13.2x interest. Floating-rate exposure has been eliminated. Stock compensation of $8,785m over the trailing twelve months is 11.6% of revenue, with $20,106m unrecognized, and the share count has risen in each of the last two fiscal years and in the first half of FY2026 despite $8,450m of repurchases.

11. Key person and a CFO handover at the point of maximum commitment. Hock Tan is named in Item 1A, none of senior management is under a written employment contract, and there is no key-person insurance. Kirsten Spears retired on 12 June 2026 after twelve years. The handover quarter is the one in which purchase commitments went from $54m to $128,110m and the $29bn backstop was signed.

12. Non-AI as a flat base. Roughly $17bn annualized, about 19% of the FQ2 run-rate and shrinking as a share, and wireless is the component with the realized in-sourcing precedent.

How these correlate. One event sets off four of these at once. If one of the six AI customers defers or cancels, the $128.1bn of purchase commitments does not move, so wafer, memory and rack inventory arrives against revenue that does not, and an inventory charge becomes the route by which the commitment reaches the income statement. The customer most likely to defer is the one whose lease obligations Broadcom backstops, because that is the customer with the weakest independent credit, so the $29bn exposure and the order deferral are one event. Collections concentrate at the same time, because one distributor is 42% of net revenue. And AI networking mix falls back toward 30% while accelerator volume slows, so gross margin declines alongside revenue instead of cushioning it. Software and semiconductors are not independent offsets either, because the FQ3 software step depends on recognition timing in the same quarter.

Predecessor-registrant annual reports for Avago Technologies Limited FY2015 (CIK 0001441634) and Broadcom Limited FY2016 (CIK 0001649338) were pulled from EDGAR and recorded to the archive. Transcripts. Forty-six quarterly earnings calls, FQ1 FY2015 through FQ2 FY2026, with no gaps, plus fifteen non-earnings events including the 2021 investor day, the 2024 investor meeting, three 2021-2022 segment teach-ins, and the acquisition announcement calls for Broadcom Corporation, Brocade, Symantec and VMware. The FQ2 FY2026 file is a machine transcript with proper-noun errors; names are corrected in every quotation here and no such token is reproduced.

Peer and value-chain filings, from the archive: NVIDIA, Marvell, AMD, Arista, Astera Labs, Credo, Qualcomm, Skyworks, Qorvo, Cisco, Nutanix, Microsoft, IBM, TSMC (20-F and 6-K), ASE Technology (20-F and 6-K), Amkor, Alphabet, Meta and Micron. Market and estimate data. Bloomberg via xBBG against the live terminal on 14 August 2026: daily prices, total-return index, forward consensus by fiscal year and one-year-forward overrides, quarterly consensus at each print, announcement dates and surprises, analyst recommendations and targets, a 536-company base-rate panel covering FY1995-FY2025, peer forward consensus, and the 33-column comparable-company table. Dated copies are archived. A local sell-side digest supplied six Broadcom-covering reports.

Series constructed from the sources above. A ten-year annual financial series and a twelve-quarter series reconciled line by line to the filings; a two-equation solve for AI and non-AI gross margin from filed segment revenue and cost of revenue; an accelerator bill-of-materials stack; a 27-driver forward model with bear, base and bull cases and a seven-driver sensitivity table; and four market charts.

Gaps and failures.

  • MediaTek and Alchip file in Taiwan and have no EDGAR registration, so their gross margin, operating margin, R&D intensity and return on invested capital are absent from the Section 3 peer table. They are the two ASIC houses that have taken sockets from a Broadcom customer.
  • IDC's worldwide virtual-machine and endpoint-security share reports are paywalled and returned HTTP 403, so vendor share percentages for those two markets are built bottom-up from company filings instead.
  • The 650 Group and Dell'Oro primary Ethernet switch silicon share reports are paywalled, so the roughly 80% share figure for merchant AI Ethernet switching comes from secondary trade coverage and is not relied on here.
  • Samsung's own newsroom release on the July 2026 memorandum of understanding did not fetch directly on two attempts and is tagged [web, unverified], from a search summary and a sell-side note. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have no EDGAR registration, so the memory counterparty's side of the arrangement is web-only.
  • SEC EDGAR's ownership browse returned HTTP 403, and the local Form 4 store covers only 4 March to 23 April 2026, so Hock Tan's calendar-2025 sales are cited from secform4.com, which reconciles exactly to the 2026 proxy's share count, and the September and mid-December 2025 trades are [web, unverified] from aggregators.
  • Bloomberg's own Broadcom history contains three errors that were corrected before use and that would flip conclusions if left: IS_EPS is basic and not diluted, overstating FY2025 GAAP EPS by 2.9%; annual IS_COMP_EPS_ADJUSTED disagrees with Broadcom's reported non-GAAP EPS before FY2022 (FY2021 1.581 against 2.800); and the stored FQ3 FY2024 consensus EPS was re-based by the July 2024 split from 1.215 to 1.563, which turns a 2.1% beat into a 21% miss. The pre-split print is used and dated.
  • A local metrics store attributes Broadcom's annual segment revenue and adjusted EBITDA one fiscal year early, so those series come from the 10-K and the calls directly; its quarterly series checks against the 10-Qs.
  • Bloomberg's EBITDA for Broadcom runs $91m to $187m above the build from filed operating income plus filed depreciation and amortization in every year from FY2020, the year the cash-flow caption changed to include right-of-use amortization. The definitional cause is not identifiable from the disclosures, and the filed build is used.
  • The Bloomberg FY2028 revenue low of $54,428m and EPS low of $15.77 are stale contributor records and are excluded from the dispersion discussion.
  • Segment cost of revenue is disclosed only from FY2023 under the expanded segment-expense standard, so segment gross-margin history begins there while segment operating margin extends to FY2018.

Discrepancies left unresolved. Management's consolidated backlog of $162bn against filed remaining performance obligations of $33.3bn on the same date. The two management values for FY2023 AI revenue, $4.2bn implied and $3.8bn stated. Management's days-of-inventory measure (58, 68, 86) against the same quarters computed from filed inventory and cost of revenue (36, 44, 58), where direction and proportional change agree and the level does not and the basis is undisclosed. FY2024 stock compensation of $5,741m in the cash-flow statement against $5,670m in the management discussion, the difference being discontinued operations. Three rating agencies publishing three FY2025 leverage figures spanning 0.8 of a turn. And Broadcom's mainframe market of "about $7 billion" against IBM's Transaction Processing line alone running roughly $8bn a year, which describes a different market boundary.

And Appendix A's patent bullet pairs a 14% decline over 21 months with R&D "roughly doubled", which happened over the 2018-to-2026 span and not the 21 months; over 21 months R&D rose about 28%.

Two duplications are left in place because the sections disagree about which owns them: §18's risk 8 opens with the tax sentence §13.3 already carries verbatim, and §18's risk 10 restates §12's tangible-book and dilution paragraphs almost word for word. §18 needs the dollar figures to justify its ranking and §12 needs them to describe the capital structure, so the cut is an editorial decision and not a numerical one.

Five are two-equation or residual solves on filed segment data (AI and non-AI gross margin; accelerator and networking gross margin; the software line split; the software geographic split; the non-VMware growth rate). Three are bottom-up unit or bill-of-materials builds (accelerator units and price; the accelerator input-cost stack; networking content per accelerator). Two are ratio applications to a disclosed base (segment invested capital and return on capital; receivable concentration at the latest balance). And two are third-party-model arithmetic, both flagged as directional because both inputs are forecasts (the share-loss exposure at Google; total infrastructure cost per gigawatt).

20. What we still don't know, and what would resolve it

Nine gaps are material enough to change a conclusion above.

  1. Broadcom's share of Google's TPU volume. Published estimates span 65% to 95%, the April 2026 agreement's value and any volume commitment are undisclosed, and Alphabet publishes nothing. It is the largest component of the top-ranked driver in Section 17. Resolved by: an 8-K with contract terms, a disclosed unit or dollar commitment, or Alphabet's own accelerator-supply disclosure.

  2. What the $128,110m of purchase commitments buys, from whom, and at what price basis. The split between memory, substrates, advanced packaging and wafers determines whether FY2027 segment gross margin holds near 69% or falls toward the mid-50s, and whether Broadcom committed at or near the cyclical peak in memory pricing that Micron's take-or-pay language describes. Resolved by: the FQ3 FY2026 commitments table, an MD&A discussion, or a named counterparty agreement.

  3. Whether the $164.6bn of remaining performance obligations and the $128,110m of purchase commitments attach to the same programme. If they do, the implied lifetime gross margin on that programme is about 22%. If they do not, $128.1bn of binding purchases stands against uncontracted revenue. Nothing published distinguishes them.

  4. Whether AI revenue is recognized on shipment into the channel or on deployment. Title for most products transfers in Penang, one unnamed distributor is 42% of net revenue and was 44% of net receivables, days of inventory went 58 to 86 in two quarters with finished goods up 2.7x, and the 10-Q states that distributors are not subject to minimum sales requirements. Together those allow reported AI revenue to lead end demand with channel inventory invisible, which bears on the reliability of the metric the model, consensus and the CEO's equity award all depend on.

  5. The identity of the distributor at 42% of net revenue, and whether AI volume flows through it. Named once, in the FQ1 FY2024 10-Q, and unnamed since. The credit-concentration question depends entirely on the answer.

  6. Which sites, utilities, interconnection queues and energization dates stand behind the roughly 10 GW planned for 2027. Power is management's terminal explanation for volume and is the most sensitive input in the model; the evidentiary base for it is one market-level datapoint. Resolved by: customer-level site and interconnection disclosure, or a utility filing.

  7. The scope of the ">$100 billion" FY2027 AI figure and the content per gigawatt inside it. Whether racks sold into the Apollo and Blackstone vehicle are inside or outside that number is not stated, and the disclosed data supports roughly $10bn per gigawatt against the $15-20bn management continues to cite. The gap is $50-100bn of FY2027 revenue.

  8. Non-AI revenue by end market. Last disclosed on the FQ4 FY2024 call in December 2024, so wireless, broadband, server storage and industrial have been dark for six quarters while the aggregate stayed flat, and which line is recovering and which is being designed out is unknown. A single quarterly end-market disclosure would fix it; without it the non-AI unit economics cannot be built and the non-AI competitive comparison uses FY2024 figures.

  9. Whether Broadcom retains AI networking content on racks whose accelerator it loses. The technology and business-model evidence establishes that Tomahawk sells into non-Broadcom accelerator and GPU footprints. If networking is retained, the $33-42bn exposure sized for a 30-point share loss at Google is roughly a third too large and the margin effect runs the opposite way, because networking is the richer half.

Six further gaps limit specific sections without changing their conclusions: MediaTek's and Alchip's returns are absent from the Section 3 peer table; whether Broadcom is bidding on Amazon's Trainium or Microsoft's Maia is unestablished, so the addressable customer set in Section 17 may be six of six or six of eight; how one dollar of end-customer AI spend splits across substrate, foundry, memory, packaging, silicon, system vendor and operator is undisclosed; the terms on which the Apollo and Blackstone vehicle buys silicon, and whether Broadcom holds equity, residual or profit participation beyond the backstop, are undisclosed; the level of software ARR and its definition are given nowhere, which is what leaves the 8-to-18-point ARR-against-revenue gap unresolved; and cost-synergy targets for LSI, PLX and Emulex were never published, so the return on those three deals cannot be computed.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Twenty-two investor decks span May 2015 to June 2026. Twelve are quarterly company overviews that restate the filings; the material ones are five acquisition announcements, three sell-side teach-ins in 2021-2022 and two investor events in 2021 and 2024. Broadcom published no quarterly investor deck between FQ3 FY2018 and FQ3 FY2025.

None of the following appears in a filing.

  • Franchise revenue, and only once. Two teach-ins three months apart attached dollars to end markets for FY2020: broadband at about $3bn, roughly 13% of revenue, and storage plus Fibre Channel at about $4bn, roughly 17%. The storage figure spans both reportable segments, because the Fibre Channel wedge is drawn inside Infrastructure Software, so a semiconductor-only end-market bridge built from it double-counts. These are the only franchise-level revenue figures Broadcom has published and they are five years old. (§1)
  • The pre-AI base for the accelerator business. The April 2022 teach-in charted custom ASIC revenue from FY2012 to FY2021: compute offload from about $0.29bn to about $1.50bn and routing and switching from about $0.15bn to about $0.78bn, each compounding 20%, for about $2.28bn in total. Compute offload rose from roughly $0.32bn in FY2016 to roughly $0.82bn in FY2017, which is the first hyperscaler accelerator programme reaching volume. AI ASICs in production went 3 in 2018, 5 in 2020 and 9 in 2022. (§1, §2)
  • What Broadcom owns inside a customer's accelerator. The 2024 investor meeting drew the division of labour explicitly: the customer owns the processing-unit architecture, and Broadcom owns the design flow and performance optimization, the HBM physical layer and integration, the network IO architecture and full-solution chiplets, and the 2.5D, 3D and silicon-photonics packaging. The next slide showed one customer at ten years and ten co-developed accelerators and a second at four years and four, both with the following generation already in architecture, on a 7-to-9-month design-to-tape-out cycle plus a three-month ramp. This is the mechanism behind the switching-cost claim. (§2, §3)
  • The served market inside an AI system. Broadcom's shaded served market covers the accelerators, both PCIe switches, all four NICs and the scale-up switch, leaving only the two CPUs; across the network it covers top-of-rack, leaf and spine switching plus the optical interconnect. Broadcom sells the rack around the accelerator whether or not it sells the accelerator, which is why the networking half runs above management's expected share and at the richer margin. (§4, §5)
  • The software acquisition playbook, quantified. CA plus Symantec Enterprise before acquisition ran about 85% gross margin, 17% R&D and 29% sales and marketing for about 39% operating margin excluding corporate overhead; the same assets inside Broadcom ran about 91%, about 14%, about 7% and about 70%. Sales and marketing falling from 29% to 7% of revenue is 22 of the 31 points of margin gain, R&D 3 and gross margin 6. The Symantec deck is unusually explicit about the path from $350m of standalone EBITDA to about $1.3bn, which runs through a deliberate revenue-optimization reduction. (§1, §10, §11)
  • Software customer concentration, disclosed once. The 2021 investor day published an ARR-weighted account pyramid: about 100 platinum accounts at 44% of ARR, 200 gold at 19%, 300 silver at 11%, 6,000-plus enterprise at 20% and 100,000-plus commercial at 6%. About 600 strategic accounts produced over 70% of ARR and 96 accounts each produced $10m or more. No update has been published. (§1, §18)
  • Backlog grows on contract length before it grows on recurring revenue. Across FQ4 FY2020 to FQ3 FY2021, ARR rose 4.2% from $4.96bn to $5.17bn while renewable backlog rose 11.6% from $12.9bn to $14.4bn and stated average deal duration rose 44% from 1.6 to 2.3 years. That is the same mechanism behind the $73bn software backlog cited at FY2025 year-end against $49bn a year earlier, and it is why a backlog figure and an ARR growth rate are not substitutes. (§1, §8)
  • Mainframe share. Gartner data at the 2021 investor day put Broadcom at 37% of a "$7bn+" mainframe software market against IBM at 25% and BMC at 19%, so Broadcom holds a larger share than the company that builds the mainframe. At 37% of $7bn that implies roughly $2.6bn of mainframe revenue, a minimum because the market figure is stated as a floor. (§4)
  • Unit share and installed base across the mature franchises. Sole global supplier of DSL infrastructure semiconductors since 2015 and over 70% of high-performance VDSL customer-premises SoCs since 2010; over 80% of Wi-Fi 6 access-point infrastructure; over one billion set-top-box and 500 million cable-modem SoCs shipped; data protection in 70% of enterprise servers; about 60% Fibre Channel host-bus-adapter share and about 70% switch share held for a decade on a 43-million-port installed base where roughly 90% of demand is replacement on a five-year cycle. Fibre Channel port price rose from about $250 in 2011 to about $330 by 2019 as the mix moved 8G to 16G to 32G, which held revenue up while port volume did not grow. (§2, §3, §4)
  • ASIC platform scale. 90-plus ASICs delivered on 16nm, 40-plus on 7nm, 20-plus on 5nm and 10 on 3nm, with about 60 designs running concurrently and 120 tape-outs a year, and a new technology platform roughly every two years in step with the foundry. Design parameters for the complex parts were already 600-800 mm² dies, 60-110bn transistors, 96-128 GB of memory and 30-50 Tb of network bandwidth in 2.5D packaging in April 2022. (§2, §3)
  • The growth headline is arithmetic off a $48m base. Three teach-in decks opened with the same claim and the multiplier moved from 84x growth in operating profit (2009 to 2020) to 177x (2009 to 2021) in one year, while non-GAAP operating income rose 23%. Reconciling to GAAP explains it: FY2020 GAAP operating income of $4,014m divided by 84 and FY2021's $8,519m divided by 177 both give about $48m [estimate: implied FY2009 GAAP operating income from the two ratios], so the headline moved on amortization roll-off. The franchise count in the same three decks was reported as 25, then 23, then 22 inside twelve months. (§10)
  • The disclosed patent estate has been declining. From "at a glance" slides: about 21,000 patents in 2018, over 20,000 in 2021, about 21,000 in September 2024, about 20,000 in September 2025, about 19,000 in December 2025 and about 18,000 in June 2026, a 14% decline over the 21 months in which R&D roughly doubled. (§2)
  • Who runs the divisions. The company-overview decks published a full divisional general-manager roster from 2018 through December 2025, when it was split into semiconductor and software rosters with no software group president named. Both roster slides were removed in March 2026 and corporate leadership expanded to include Ram Velaga as President, Infrastructure Software Group. The general manager of the Tomahawk and Jericho franchise moved to run the software segment, and Broadcom stopped publishing who runs its divisions. (§10)
  • The VMware rationale has been overtaken. The May 2022 deck built its case on a revenue mix chart: $15.6bn at the Broadcom Corporation close, $27.5bn in FY2021 at 74% semiconductors and 26% software, and $40.1bn pro forma at 51% and 49%, headlined "balanced portfolio, growth at scale". FY2025 came in at 57.7% and 42.3% and FQ2 FY2026 at 68% and 32%. The deal works on its own EBITDA terms; the diversification argument that justified it has been overtaken by the other segment's growth. (§11)

Appendix C — External data sources

Seven external datasets bear on Broadcom's analysis. None is pulled here; each entry says what it is, what it measures and which section it would strengthen.

DRAM and NAND spot and contract pricing (mosaic). A price series for memory assembled from scattered published points, since the primary vendor series are paid. It measures the direction and level of memory contract pricing. For Broadcom this is an input-cost series: memory is between a fifth and a quarter of the accelerator selling price at contract rates, the $128,110m of purchase commitments is probably mostly memory, and Micron's take-or-pay language implies a ceiling near the second-quarter 2026 market price. It would strengthen the driver-two cost analysis in §1 and the operational-KPI discussion in §13. Partial mosaic, not comprehensive. Not pulled.

Search-interest trends (Google Trends). Relative search interest for a company and its products over time and against named peers, indexed 0-100 on a relative scale. For Broadcom the usable queries are the product names — Tomahawk, Jericho, VMware Cloud Foundation — and VMware-migration intent, which would give a demand signal for a business whose customer behaviour is otherwise invisible between quarterly calls. It would strengthen §6 on the software installed base and §4 on the private-cloud landscape. Not pulled.

Hiring and headcount signals (job postings, professional-network counts, layoff trackers). Open-role counts by function, total posting trend, and announced headcount actions. The informative cut for Broadcom is design and verification engineering headcount against the count of accelerator programmes, which is the direct test of the §2 question about whether the reusable design flow lets a shrinking R&D line serve seventeen divisions or whether the engineering base is being underfunded; and post-acquisition software headcount actions against the §3.2 finding that margin expansion is funded by cost removal. It would strengthen §1, §2 and §18. Not pulled.

Developer-ecosystem adoption (package downloads, code-hosting activity, developer surveys). Adoption and momentum of a vendor's tooling among developers. For Broadcom the relevant series are VMware and Tanzu tooling and any open Ethernet or SerDes ecosystem activity. It is a weaker fit than for a platform vendor, because Broadcom's software is sold to infrastructure operators and not to developers. It would inform §1 and §6. Not pulled.

Internet traffic and application telemetry (Cloudflare Radar, Similarweb). Third-party telemetry on internet and application traffic, including AI crawler share. For Broadcom the useful measure is aggregate AI and data-centre traffic growth as a demand backdrop for switching and optical silicon, and not company-specific usage. It would inform §6. Partial mosaic, not comprehensive. Not pulled.

Web technology and CDN adoption share (W3Techs, BuiltWith, HTTP Archive). The share of public websites running a vendor's product over time. This maps loosely onto Broadcom, whose software is enterprise virtualization, mainframe and security. It would show the adoption of web-facing technologies and say nothing about VMware estate share. It is listed for completeness. Not pulled.

Service reliability and outage incidents (status pages, outage trackers). Frequency and severity of vendor outages. Broadcom's software is largely customer-operated on-premises, so vendor uptime is not the product in the way it is for a hosted service, and this series would say little. Not pulled.
